properties.Title: innflow Devin Integration for Property Workflows

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Add an innflow Cursor integration in mcp.json so agent mode can inspect and run deployed property workflows, with OAuth scopes and a person still on send.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders and the engineers who support them
properties.draft_blog:
Agent mode in the editor needs a workflow it can name

Cursor is where a lot of property engineers now review a change: a template, a script, a checklist, a small internal tool. Agent mode can edit that project and call MCP servers configured for it. An innflow Cursor integration is the missing name. The agent can list the workflows in a workspace, inspect the one you mean, and run it only after it is deployed.

innflow is the operations layer: AI workflows on a visible canvas, with handoffs and permissions you can see. The property management system stays the system of record. Cursor stays the editor. Neither one has to pretend to be the other.

This guide shows the project config, the sign-in, a leasing example, and the API path for anything that should run without the editor open.

What you want Cursor to touch

A leasing change often starts as a sentence. "The applicant packet needs the pet addendum field." That sentence becomes a checklist edit, sometimes a workflow edit, and always a question about what production currently expects. Cursor is a good place to hold the sentence next to the files.

It is a bad place to invent the production state. The deployed workflow is the production state. An innflow Cursor integration lets the agent read it. The person still decides whether today's diff is allowed to deploy.

Keep messages to applicants out of agent mode. The workflow can prepare them. The leasing owner sends them from innflow.

The actions behind the connection

Point Cursor at https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp. Authentication is OAuth 2.1. You select a workspace and approve scopes. The grant is revocable and it is not an API key.

After approval the agent can:

  • List workflows
  • Inspect one workflow
  • Execute a deployed workflow
  • Deploy a workflow or return it to draft
  • List executions
  • Read execution details and node logs

A draft will not run. A read-only member will not get write calls. If agent mode insists, the platform is correct and the prompt is wrong.

For a runner outside the editor, use https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1 with a key from Settings: API Keys. Keys start with inf_sk_ and are shown once. The API introduction documents workspaces, idempotency, and errors.

X-Innflow-Workspace selects an organization workspace. Idempotency-Key makes create, import, duplicate, deploy, undeploy, and execute safe to retry when the body is unchanged. A different body with the same key conflicts on purpose.

Project config that can be committed

Create .cursor/mcp.json in the repo:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "innflow": {
      "url": "https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp"
    }
  }
}

If the editor asks for a transport, choose HTTP, the streamable HTTP form. Save the file. Open agent mode and ask it to list innflow tools. Finish sign-in in the browser, pick the workspace, and approve scopes.

Commit the JSON. Do not commit a token, a bearer header, or an inf_sk_ value. The URL is not a secret. The grant is.

A global Cursor MCP entry is fine for one person hopping repos. The project file is better when a teammate should see the same server name on a fresh clone. They still sign in as themselves.

Add a few lines where Cursor already reads project rules. List and inspect are the default. Execute needs a workflow name and a person. Deploy needs a second yes. Applicant, resident, owner, and vendor messages stay in innflow.

Worked example: the pet addendum field

The packet workflow is deployed. Leasing wants a pet addendum flag on the input. The checklist in the repo does not mention it yet. Production logs from last week show the old input shape.

  1. Ask Cursor to inspect the deployed packet workflow and list inputs.
  2. Ask it to show one recent successful execution so you can see a real payload, not a guessed one.
  3. Edit the checklist in the repo. Review the diff yourself.
  4. Change the canvas in innflow only when leasing has agreed the new field is required.
  5. Deploy that change as its own step, with its own idempotency key if you deploy through the API.
  6. Execute a single test applicant that leasing has marked as safe to retry. Read the new log.
  7. Leave the applicant email on the canvas.

A prompt that matches the first step: "Using the innflow connection, inspect the applicant packet workflow and quote its input fields. Do not deploy or execute." That is the tone of a sane innflow Cursor integration. Curiosity first, state change second.

Agent mode likes to be helpful and finish the whole list. Stop it between inspect and deploy. The gap is where a person looks at the canvas.

A runner for the cases that are not interactive

After the field exists, a small script can execute the deployed workflow for a batch leasing already approved. The script uses a key.

curl -X POST https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows/{workflowId}/execute \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: packet-2026-09-29-applicant-88" \
  -d '{"input":{"applicantId":"88","petAddendum":true}}'

Cursor can write this script. It should not embed the key. Read the key from the environment. On failure, store requestId and X-Request-Id with the applicant id so the next person can find the same error.

Expire the key. Revoke it if a debug log prints it. The settings page shows last used time, which is enough to see whether a forgotten runner is still alive.

When the call fails, and the other MCP direction

Unauthorized means the grant is missing. Finish OAuth. A read-only error means you are inspecting with the right role and you tried to write. Switch role only if that person should deploy. A draft error means the canvas was never deployed. An idempotency conflict means the key does not match this body. Look at the previous response before you send a new one.

There is also an outward connection. Settings: MCP servers plus an MCP node lets a workflow call tools on some other server. Use that when the packet workflow needs an outside tool. Use the Cursor connection when a person in the editor needs the packet workflow. Write both down in the runbook under different names.

AES-256 applies in transit and at rest. Customer content is not kept for model training. Private and VPC deployment stay available. The mcp.json entry does not change those terms.

innflow is trusted by 1,260+ real estate professionals. The check you can do this afternoon is smaller: the input list in Cursor matches the canvas, and the applicant still hears from leasing inside innflow.

A review ritual that survives agent mode

Cursor will try to finish the whole leasing change in one turn. The ritual is a set of stops. Stop after the input list. Stop after the sample execution. Stop after the checklist diff. Stop again before deploy. Say the stop out loud in the prompt so the transcript shows it.

Keep a short project rule file the editor already reads. Name the packet workflow. Say that inspect is allowed, execute needs the applicant id in the prompt, and deploy needs a second message from a person. Say that applicant email is sent from innflow. Repeat the rule when someone new clones the repo. The mcp.json file gets them the server. The rule gets them the manners.

Once a week, compare three artifacts: the input list from inspect, a real execution payload, and the checklist in git. They should describe the same fields. When they drift, the checklist is wrong or the canvas changed without a note. Fix the drift before the next applicant. An innflow Cursor integration that is not checked against a real payload becomes a confident guess.

Practice one refusal. Ask agent mode to execute while the workflow is a draft, on a sandbox workflow you control. Read the error together. Teams that have seen the refusal do not argue with it later, during a live tour day.

If two leasing coordinators share one workspace, agree who executes. The other person may inspect. Shared execute rights plus two open Cursor windows is how duplicate packets happen. Idempotency keys help only when both people use the same key scheme. Write the scheme down: applicant id, workflow slug, and the date.

At the end of the change, leave the canvas deployed state in the pull request description. Reviewers should see whether this diff also required a deploy. A merged checklist with an undeployed canvas is an incomplete change, even if the code looks finished.

A weekly audit you can finish in twenty minutes

Pick one afternoon. Open the repo and the canvas. Ask Cursor to list the workflows this project is allowed to call. The allowed list should be one or two names, written in the project rules. Extra names are a sign the grant is wider than the work.

For the packet workflow, copy the input fields from inspect into the audit note. Open the newest successful execution and copy the keys that were actually sent. Diff them against the checklist. Three columns, one row per field: documented, inspected, executed. A field in only one column is the week's fix. Do not start a new feature while a column is empty.

Read the last error, if there is one. Save the request id in the note. Say whether it was unauthorized, a draft, a read-only role, or an idempotency conflict. Those four are the ones this integration is built to produce. Any other error gets the request id and a person, not another prompt that hopes the next try works.

Check git history for .cursor/mcp.json. The diff should only ever show the server name and the URL. If a token appeared, even briefly, revoke the credential and scrub the history with the person who owns the repo. Then look at who still has OAuth access to the workspace. Remove anyone who left the leasing project.

End the audit by naming the sender. One role sends applicant messages from innflow. If the note says "the agent," the audit failed. Write the person's role, not a model name. That single line keeps an innflow Cursor integration from drifting into an unsupervised mailbox.

When the audit finds a drift, fix it in the same afternoon if you can. A field that exists on the canvas and not in git will be missed by the next applicant. A field that exists in git and not on the canvas will be sent into a workflow that drops it. Either gap is a leasing error waiting for a tour day. Write the fix as a checklist change, a canvas change, or both, and deploy only the canvas half with a witness. Then re-run the three-column check on that one field so the note shows it closed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does an innflow Cursor integration replace our property management system?

No. The property management system remains the system of record for units, leases, and money. innflow runs the workflows. Cursor is the editor and the MCP client.

Will agent mode run a draft if I ask nicely?

No. Execute requires a deployed workflow. Deploy it on the canvas, then call execute.

Is it safe to commit .cursor/mcp.json?

Yes, when the file contains only the server name and the innflow URL. It is not safe once a key or a bearer token is added. Keep those out of the repo.

Can Cursor email the applicant?

Do not give the session that send. The workflow prepares the packet. Leasing sends from innflow.

How do we avoid two packet runs for one applicant?

Bind the run to an idempotency key that includes the applicant and the date or the attempt. Reuse it only for an identical retry. Change the payload, change the key.

Name the workflow before you change it

Add the config. Sign in. Inspect the packet. Read one real execution. Then decide if today's field belongs in production. That sequence is the innflow Cursor integration doing the job property teams actually have.

Open app.innflow.ai/signup to start, or app.innflow.ai if the workspace is already there.
properties.Title: innflow Cursor Integration for Property Workflows

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Use an innflow Codex integration to list, inspect, and run deployed property workflows from the terminal, with OAuth scopes and a person on the send step.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders and the engineers who support them
properties.draft_blog:
A terminal agent still needs an operations system

A property team does not run on chat. It runs on packets, notices, vendor calls, and the record of who approved the last step. Codex is a strong place to do the file work around that operation: read a repo, edit a template, and keep a command history. An innflow Codex integration is how that terminal session reaches the workflows that already know the operation.

innflow is property operations software with AI workflows. Agents run on a visible canvas. The property management system stays the system of record. Codex does not become that system, and innflow does not become the editor. The integration is the handshake between them.

This guide covers what the connection can do, how to attach Codex to the hosted MCP server, when the public API is the better path, and a worked example for an application packet. A person still owns the message that leaves the building.

What Codex is doing in a property repo

OpenAI Codex, in the CLI and in the IDE extension, is a coding harness. It plans a change, edits files, and runs commands inside a project you trust. Property teams use that shape more often than a pure software company admits.

The repo might hold notice templates, a checklist for move-in, a script that exports owner statements, or the notes an engineer keeps next to a workflow. Codex is good at that local work. It can see the files, propose a diff, and stop when you say stop.

It cannot see a deployed workflow, an execution log, or the credential boundary of a workspace unless you connect it. Pasting a screenshot of the canvas into the terminal is a slow version of the same idea. The connection makes the question direct: which workflows exist, which one is deployed, and what did the last run do.

That is the whole point of an innflow Codex integration. The harness stays in the repo. The operation stays on the canvas, where status, handoff, and permissions are visible.

What the connection is allowed to do

innflow exposes two doors.

The hosted MCP server is for harnesses that speak the Model Context Protocol. The endpoint is https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp. It uses OAuth 2.1. There is no API key on this door. Codex opens a sign-in, you pick a workspace, and you approve scopes. Access is workspace-scoped and revocable.

Once that session is authorized, Codex can do the same class of work the public API exposes:

  • List workflows in the workspace
  • Inspect one workflow
  • Run a workflow that is already deployed
  • Deploy a workflow, or return it to draft
  • List executions
  • Read execution details and node logs

A workflow that is still a draft will not execute. Read-only members of a workspace cannot use write endpoints. Those two rules matter more than the transport.

The public API is the second door, for scripts, cron, and any client that should use a key instead of an interactive sign-in. The base URL is https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1. Keys are created under Settings: API Keys. They start with inf_sk_ and the full value is shown once. The OpenAPI document lives at https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/openapi.json.

Requests default to the personal workspace. Send X-Innflow-Workspace with an organization id when the work belongs to another workspace you can access. Create, import, duplicate, deploy, undeploy, and execute accept an Idempotency-Key header. The same key and the same request replay the saved response for 24 hours. The same key with a different body returns a conflict.

Connect Codex with MCP

Codex stores MCP servers in config.toml, shared by the CLI and the IDE extension. The user file is ~/.codex/config.toml. A trusted project can also carry .codex/config.toml.

Add the server from the CLI:

codex mcp add innflow --url https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp

Or write the block yourself:

[mcp_servers.innflow]
url = "https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp"

Start Codex in the property repo and ask it to list innflow tools. The first call should send you through innflow sign-in. Pick the workspace that owns the workflows, review the scopes, and approve. If the server answers before that approval, you will see an unauthorized response. That is the connection waiting for a person, which is the correct first state.

Confirm the server is present:

codex mcp list

Then ask a narrow question. "List the workflows in this innflow workspace" is a better first prompt than "run everything." You want to see names before anyone executes.

Keep secrets out of the repo. The OAuth grant lives with the Codex sign-in. Do not copy an inf_sk_ key into config.toml and commit it. If a key has already leaked, revoke it under Settings: API Keys and create a new one.

A short note in AGENTS.md helps the session stay inside the boundary: use the innflow server to list and inspect workflows, execute only a named deployed workflow, and never send resident, owner, or vendor messages from the terminal. The send step stays in innflow.

When the public API is the better door

MCP fits an interactive Codex session. A nightly job is a different shape. Nobody is sitting at the sign-in window at 2 a.m.

For that job, create a key with a real expiration. Thirty days is enough for a trial. Ninety days or one year fits a stable script. "Never" is available and should be rare. Store the key in the secret store the job already uses. Pass it only as Authorization: Bearer.

A list call looks like this:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows

An execute call is allowed only after deploy:

curl -X POST https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows/{workflowId}/execute \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: application-packet-2026-09-29-unit-12" \
  -d '{"input":{"applicantEmail":"applicant@example.com"}}'

The response includes the workflow id, event ids, and a triggered status. Failures return JSON with a human-readable error, an optional code, and a requestId. The X-Request-Id header is the value to hand to support.

Use the API from Codex when the session is writing a script. Use MCP when the session is the operator. Mixing them in one prompt, with a key pasted into chat, is how keys leak.

Worked example: the application packet

A leasing coordinator finishes a tour. The applicant exists in the property management system. What the team still does by hand is the packet: pull the checklist, confirm the documents the workflow expects, and prepare the internal handoff. That packet is a deployed innflow workflow. The coordinator's engineer keeps the checklist copy in a repo Codex can read.

The session starts with inspection, not execution.

  1. Ask Codex to list workflows and name the application-packet workflow.
  2. Ask it to inspect that workflow so the required input fields are visible.
  3. Compare those fields to the checklist in the repo. If a field is missing, stop. Fix the input or the canvas. Do not execute a half-built payload.
  4. When the fields match, ask Codex to execute the deployed workflow with one applicant's input and a fresh idempotency key.
  5. Ask it to read the execution log. The log is the record. A cheerful summary is not.
  6. The person who owns leasing sends any applicant-facing message from innflow.

A prompt that respects the boundary sounds like this: "Using the innflow connection, inspect the deployed application packet workflow. Tell me the input fields. Do not execute yet." The second prompt, after a person agrees, names the workflow id and the input. The third prompt reads the new execution.

If Codex offers to email the applicant from the terminal, decline. Drafts can be prepared inside the workflow. The send stays on the canvas, where the credential and the handoff are visible.

Deploy is a separate decision. An innflow Codex integration can deploy, and it can return a workflow to draft. In the packet example, deploy belongs to the person who reviewed the canvas change. The terminal session can prepare the diff in the repo and can read logs. It should not ship a new version because the model sounded confident.

Controls, failures, and the other direction

Treat the connection like a staff login with a narrow job.

  • Approve the smallest workspace that contains the workflows this repo should see.
  • Prefer read prompts until the workflow name and the input shape are confirmed.
  • Execute only deployed workflows.
  • Put a new idempotency key on every real run. Reuse a key only when you intend to replay the same request.
  • Revoke the OAuth grant or the API key when a person leaves the repo or the role changes.

Common failures are ordinary. Unauthorized means the sign-in is not finished or the grant was revoked. A write rejected for a read-only member means the workspace role is doing its job. An execute rejected because the workflow is not deployed means the canvas is still a draft. An idempotency conflict means the key was reused with a different body. Read requestId before you retry.

There is a second direction, and it is easy to confuse with this one. Inside innflow, Settings: MCP servers registers an external MCP server, and an MCP node on the canvas can call that server's tools. That is innflow reaching out. An innflow Codex integration, as this guide uses the phrase, is Codex reaching in. Use the outward node when a workflow needs a tool Codex is not providing. Use the inward connection when a person in Codex needs the workflow.

Security on the innflow side stays in force either way. Traffic and stored data use AES-256. Model training does not retain customer data. Teams that need a private or VPC deployment can keep that boundary. The harness does not widen it.

innflow is trusted by 1,260+ real estate professionals. The useful proof in this setup is quieter: the canvas shows the flow, the log shows the run, and a person still releases anything a resident will read.

A first week that stays small

Day one is the connection and nothing else. Add the MCP server, finish OAuth, and ask Codex to list workflow names. Write those names into the repo note. If the list is empty, you are in the wrong workspace. Fix that before anyone talks about execution.

Day two is one old log. Pick a workflow the team already trusts and read a finished execution. Compare the input in the log with the checklist in the repo. Differences belong in the note. They are not a reason to execute a new run.

Day three is a single execute, on a case a person has marked as safe. Use a fresh idempotency key. Read the new log in the same session and again on the canvas. If the two views disagree, stop and keep the request id.

Day four is a failure drill. Ask Codex what an undeployed workflow does, and what a read-only member can do. You want to see the refusal. A session that cannot show you a refusal is a session you should not trust with a real packet.

Day five is the runbook paragraph: which workflow id, who may execute, who sends, and where the key lives if a script exists. That paragraph is the innflow Codex integration after the novelty wears off. The following week repeats day three. It does not add a second workflow until the first one has been boring.

Keep the API key, if you created one for a script, on a 30-day or 90-day expiration for this trial. Revoke it at the review even if you plan to create another. A key that survives its experiment becomes an unknown client.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does an innflow Codex integration replace our property management system?

No. The property management system remains the system of record. innflow runs the workflows around that record. Codex edits files and calls those workflows. Leases, ledgers, and units stay where they already live.

Can Codex execute a workflow that is still a draft?

No. Deploy the workflow on the canvas first. The API and the MCP session both refuse to execute a draft. That is the gate that keeps a terminal experiment off a live packet.

Should I paste an API key into Codex?

Use the hosted MCP sign-in for interactive sessions. Create an inf_sk_ key only for a script or a job, store it outside the repo, and revoke it if it appears in a prompt, a commit, or a log.

Can Codex email residents, owners, or vendors?

Do not give it that job. A workflow may prepare a draft. The person responsible sends it from innflow, on the credential the workspace already trusts.

What if two Codex sessions run the same packet?

Give each real run its own idempotency key. If a retry is truly the same request, reuse the key and innflow will replay the saved response for 24 hours instead of starting a second run.

Start with one deployed workflow

Pick the workflow your team already trusts. Connect Codex. List it. Inspect it. Read one old execution before you execute a new one. That sequence is the innflow Codex integration in practice: a terminal harness, a visible workflow, and a person on the step that leaves the building.

When the packet path is boring, add the next workflow. Boring is the goal.

Get started at app.innflow.ai/signup, or open the workspace you already have at app.innflow.ai. API details are in the innflow API introduction.

properties.Author: Arianna Khan
properties.description: Connect Claude Code with an innflow Claude integration to list, inspect, and run deployed property workflows, with OAuth scopes and a human send step.
properties.Audience: Property operations leaders and the engineers who support them
properties.draft_blog:
Claude Code can see the repo. The workflow lives elsewhere.

Claude Code is the terminal harness many teams already trust with a repository. It reads files, edits them, and runs commands in a project you have opened. Property work has a second surface. The renewal checklist, the handoff, and the record of the last run live on an innflow canvas. An innflow Claude integration is the connection between those surfaces when the harness is Claude Code.

This is a connection guide. It is about signing Claude Code into a workspace, listing deployed workflows, and keeping the send step with a person. innflow remains property operations software with AI workflows. The property management system remains the system of record.

If you are planning broader Claude agent workflows for support or sales, treat that as a separate design. Here, the job is narrower: a coding session that can call a workflow you have already deployed.

Why a property team opens Claude Code at all

Renewal season is a pile of files plus a pile of judgment. The files are notice language, a date calculator, a list of what the workflow must receive. The judgment is whether this resident's packet is ready. Claude Code is useful on the file pile. It can diff a template, check that a required field is mentioned, and show its work in the terminal.

It is not useful as a hidden operator. If the session cannot list workflows or read logs, people compensate by pasting. Paste drifts. The log on the canvas is the record. An innflow Claude integration lets the session read that record and, when a person says so, start a deployed run.

The canvas stays visible. Status, handoff, and permissions stay on innflow. Claude Code stays a client.

What an authorized session can do

Hosted MCP is at https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp. The protocol is OAuth 2.1. Claude Code starts the sign-in, you choose the workspace, and you approve scopes. No API key is required for this door. You can revoke the grant later.

The session can then:

  • List workflows in the workspace
  • Inspect a workflow and its inputs
  • Execute a workflow that is already deployed
  • Deploy, or undeploy back to draft
  • List executions
  • Read an execution, including node logs

Execution fails closed when the workflow is still a draft. A read-only member cannot deploy, undeploy, or execute. Hold that line even if the model is sure.

Scripts and schedulers use the public API at https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1. Keys are created in Settings: API Keys, start with inf_sk_, and appear in full only once. See the API key guide and the API introduction.

Organization work sends X-Innflow-Workspace. Writes accept Idempotency-Key. A repeated identical request replays for 24 hours. A repeated key with a different body is a conflict, which is the signal to stop and look, not to hammer the endpoint.

Add innflow to Claude Code

From the project directory:

claude mcp add --transport http innflow https://mcp.innflow.ai/mcp

Start a Claude Code session and ask it to list the innflow tools. Complete the browser sign-in. Select the workspace that owns the renewal workflows. Approve the scopes you actually want this repo to have.

Before approval, the endpoint answers unauthorized. That is expected. Do not "fix" it by pasting a key into the command history.

A project note keeps later sessions honest. Tell Claude Code to use the innflow server for list and inspect, to execute only a workflow you name, and to leave resident, owner, and vendor messages inside innflow. The note is not a permission system. The OAuth scopes and the workspace role are the permission system. The note just stops the session from wandering.

User-scoped MCP config is reasonable for one operator. Project-scoped config is reasonable when everyone who clones the repo should see the server name. The grant stays on the person either way.

Worked example: renewal prep

A community manager has a deployed workflow that prepares a renewal packet. The repo holds the notice language and a checklist of inputs: resident id, lease end, and the offer the manager already chose in the property management system. Claude Code can read the checklist. innflow can run the packet.

  1. Ask Claude Code to list workflows and point at the renewal workflow.
  2. Ask it to inspect inputs. Put that list next to the checklist file. Stop if they disagree.
  3. Fix the disagreement in the repo or on the canvas before any execute call.
  4. When a person confirms the input, execute the deployed workflow with one resident and a new idempotency key.
  5. Read the execution log back. Quote the nodes. A summary that skips the log is not done.
  6. The manager sends the resident notice from innflow.

The first prompt is deliberately dull: "Using the innflow connection, inspect the deployed renewal workflow and list its input fields. Do not execute." Dull is how an innflow Claude integration stays safe on a Tuesday.

Deploy is not part of that prompt. If the canvas needs a new field, the person who owns renewals deploys after they have seen the change. Claude Code can show a proposed edit to the checklist. It should not flip a production workflow to a new version on its own initiative.

If the session drafts an email in the terminal and offers to send it, leave the draft in the workflow. Sending is a credentialed action on the canvas.

The API path, for the job that is not a session

A Monday morning batch is not a conversation. Use a key with an expiration, stored outside the repo.

curl -X POST https://app.innflow.ai/api/v1/workflows/{workflowId}/execute \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer inf_sk_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: renewal-2026-09-29-resident-441" \
  -d '{"input":{"residentId":"441","leaseEnd":"2026-11-30"}}'

The body comes back with a triggered status, workflow id, and event ids. On failure, keep requestId and the X-Request-Id header. Claude Code can help you write this script. It should read the key from the environment, never from a chat paste.

Revoke the key when the season ends or when the person who created it changes roles. Settings shows a masked preview, last used time, and a revoke action.

Failures, scope, and calling the other way

Unauthorized: finish sign-in or restore a revoked grant. Read-only rejection: the workspace role is right, so change the role on purpose or use a member who can write. Draft rejection: deploy first. Idempotency conflict: you reused a key with a new body. Read the error before you mint another key and fire again.

innflow also has an outward MCP path. Under Settings: MCP servers you can register a server the canvas should call, then use an MCP node on the workflow. That is a workflow reaching a tool. The Claude Code connection is a person reaching a workflow. Name them differently in your runbook so an on-call engineer does not debug the wrong door.

Data in transit and at rest is encrypted with AES-256. innflow does not retain customer data for model training. Private and VPC deployment remain options. Connecting Claude Code does not relax those controls.

innflow is trusted by 1,260+ real estate professionals. For this integration, check a smaller fact: the log Claude Code reads is the log on the canvas, and the resident hears from a person using innflow.

Renewal week, kept to one workflow

Open the week by listing workflows and writing the renewal workflow id into AGENTS.md. Include the input fields you inspected, the role allowed to execute, and the name of the manager who sends. Claude Code will follow a concrete note more calmly than a vague instruction to be careful.

Each morning, inspect before anyone talks about a batch. Read yesterday's executions. A run that triggered and a run that finished are different facts. Quote the node that finished, or the node that stopped. Then decide whether today's residents are actually ready.

Execute one resident at a time until the log looks familiar. A batch script can come later, with a key and an idempotency key per resident. The interactive innflow Claude integration is the place you learn the shape. The script is the place you repeat a shape you already trust.

Midweek, try the refusal on purpose. Ask the session to execute a draft copy, or ask a read-only teammate to deploy. Save the error text in the repo note. Future you will want to recognize that text in a hurry.

End the week by revoking any trial key and confirming the OAuth grant still belongs to people who work this portfolio. Scopes linger when seasons end. The canvas does not remind you.

If a notice must change, change the template in git, review the diff, and only then touch the canvas. Deploy is a manager's action. The terminal can show the sentence. It should not publish the sentence to a resident.

What the manager should see

The terminal transcript is for the engineer. The manager needs a smaller view: which resident, which workflow, whether the run finished, and who is about to send. Put that view on the canvas, not in a pasted summary. Claude Code can read the execution and name the resident id. The manager opens the same execution and sees the nodes.

Agree on three words for status that match the product, not a private dialect. Deployed means the workflow can run. Triggered means execute was accepted. Finished means the log shows the last node complete. If the team uses other words, write the mapping once. Misnamed status is how a renewal gets announced before the packet exists.

During the season, the manager's daily question is short. "Which of today's renewals have a finished execution, and which are still waiting on me?" Claude Code can help assemble the ids. It cannot answer as the system of record. The canvas answers. If the two lists diverge, trust the canvas and file the request id from the call that diverged.

Keep resident language in the template file and on the workflow, in one approved version. When the manager edits a sentence, that edit is reviewed and then deployed by the person who owns the workflow. A clever rewrite that lives only in the terminal will not be what the resident receives, and it should not be.

Before the season ends, archive the resident ids you executed and the idempotency keys you used. The archive is a checklist, not a story. Next season starts from that list and from the same workflow id, after someone confirms the template still matches the canvas. Leave the MCP server configured. Refresh the grant only for people who will run renewals again.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is an innflow Claude integration a replacement for the property management system?

No. The property management system keeps units, leases, and ledgers. innflow runs the workflows around that system. Claude Code is the client that can list and run those workflows after a person connects it.

Can Claude Code run a workflow that was never deployed?

No. Deploy on the canvas first. The MCP session and the API both require a deployed workflow before execute.

Do I put an API key in the claude mcp command?

Not for the hosted server. The command points at the URL. OAuth collects the grant. Use an inf_sk_ key only for a non-interactive script, and keep it out of the shell history you share.

Can the session text a resident?

Do not set it up that way. The workflow can prepare the notice. The manager sends it from innflow.

How do I stop a double renewal run?

One idempotency key per real request. An identical retry replays the saved response for 24 hours. A changed payload needs a new key.

Connect it, then inspect before you run

Add the server. Sign in. Inspect one renewal workflow. Read an old execution. Only then execute a new one, with a person still responsible for the notice. That is a complete innflow Claude integration for a property team.

Start at app.innflow.ai/signup or continue in app.innflow.ai.

properties.draft_blog:
Claude agents with innflow can be planned around the work that happens between a conversation and its next step. A customer asks a question. A meeting creates a commitment. An internal request arrives without enough detail. Someone has to gather context, identify what matters, and prepare a response or handoff.

Those are useful places to begin designing an agent workflow. The task is specific, the input already exists, and a teammate can usually explain what a good result looks like. You can test the proposed workflow against real examples before giving it a larger role in daily operations.

This guide presents seven proposed use cases across support, sales, meetings, and internal operations. They are implementation patterns, not claims about prebuilt templates or measured customer outcomes. Confirm Claude access, supported integrations, and the required actions in your innflow workspace before building them. Each example identifies the input, expected output, review boundary, and a practical way to judge success.

How to plan Claude agents with innflow

Anthropic documents Claude's ability to request tool calls for external functions. For client tools, the application executes the operation and returns its result. That is the basic connection between reasoning about a task and interacting with another system.

innflow's public workflow model emphasizes connected conversations, relevant business context, focused agent instructions, and team review. Together, those concepts suggest a practical design: give the agent a bounded preparation task, make its evidence visible, and assign a person to the next action. The exact integration path must be verified for the workspace.

Write a short task contract before configuring anything. Specify what starts the work, what information can be used, what the agent should produce, and what it must leave unresolved. Include the destination of the result. A summary without a reader or a next step often becomes another item someone has to organize.

Choose the model after defining that contract. If you are evaluating a new Claude release, use the same workflow examples and acceptance criteria across configurations. A model's reputation cannot tell you whether it handles your team's missing fields, ambiguous requests, or unusual terminology.

1. Prepare customer support replies

Trigger: a new support request enters an approved queue. Context: the conversation, relevant help material, and the customer's permitted account details. Output: a concise issue summary, supporting references, and an unsent reply for the support owner.

Imagine a customer saying that a recurring report contains an unexpected total. Ask the agent to identify the period, the reported discrepancy, and the information needed to investigate. If the source material explains a known setting, the draft can point to that explanation. If it does not, the agent should ask a precise follow-up question.

Keep promises about refunds, product fixes, and delivery dates outside the initial task. A support teammate should confirm those commitments. The useful result is a reply that accurately represents the request and reduces the effort of preparing the next response.

Measure accepted drafts, material corrections, and reviewer time. Review a sample of apparently successful cases as well as rejected ones. An incorrect assumption can sound natural enough to escape a quick check, particularly when the customer has described the issue informally.

2. Turn meetings into actionable follow-ups

Trigger: approved meeting notes become available. Context: the notes, participant names, and the project's existing decisions. Output: a recap separating decisions, proposed ideas, open questions, and explicit commitments.

Consider a project call where one person suggests a launch date and another agrees to investigate a dependency. The recap should preserve that distinction. A suggestion is not an agreed deadline. An investigation is not a promise to complete the implementation. Ask the agent to include evidence for owners and dates.

The meeting owner reviews the recap before it becomes a task list or an external email. If a deadline or owner is missing, show it as unresolved. That gives the reviewer a small set of specific decisions instead of a polished plan built on assumptions.

Evaluate whether the recap captures the commitments people actually made. Track corrections to ownership and timing separately from stylistic edits. The first categories affect coordination; the second may simply reflect an individual's writing preferences. This distinction keeps the evaluation focused on useful work.

3. Prepare sales handoffs without inventing intent

Trigger: an inquiry or discovery conversation is ready for a sales owner. Context: approved notes, known account information, and the team's routing rules. Output: a brief describing the stated need, relevant constraints, unanswered questions, and recommended next conversation.

A prospect may mention two teams, a manual reporting process, and a desire to start soon. The agent can organize those facts. It should not turn them into a confirmed budget, a purchase commitment, or a precise implementation deadline. Separate direct statements from reasonable questions for the next call.

Have the account owner review routing and any proposed CRM update. For an initial trial, let the workflow prepare the update without writing it. Compare the prepared handoff with what the receiving salesperson actually needed when continuing the conversation.

A useful measure is the number of clarification loops between the originating and receiving teams. Also inspect missing requirements. Speed is valuable only when the next person receives the context needed to move forward. A fast handoff that omits a critical constraint can create a slower process overall.

4. Triage internal service requests

Trigger: an employee submits an internal request. Context: the request text, service categories, and approved routing instructions. Output: a suggested category, a summary of missing information, and a proposed owner or queue.

For example, an employee asks for access to a reporting tool but does not name the workspace or explain the purpose. The agent's useful job is to gather those details and prepare the request for the right team. Access approval remains with the authorized owner of the system.

Build the first version around a small set of categories. Include a clear route for requests that do not fit. Avoid forcing every message into an existing label, because incorrect routing can make the queue look tidy while delaying the person who needs help.

Measure routing corrections and the time spent collecting missing details. Review whether the agent asks questions already answered in the original request. Good triage should reduce repetitive exchanges and preserve context for the person who ultimately performs the work.

5. Assemble project status briefs

Trigger: a scheduled review or a request from a project owner. Context: approved task updates, decision notes, and the current milestone plan. Output: a brief listing completed work, open dependencies, changed assumptions, and questions needing a decision.

Suppose several contributors report progress in separate conversations. Ask the agent to connect each update to the relevant milestone and retain its date. An older optimistic update should not override a more recent blocker. If the evidence conflicts, the brief should show the conflict.

Keep the project owner responsible for the final assessment. The agent should prepare the evidence, not infer that a project is healthy because most updates sound positive. Require concrete references for statements about completion, ownership, and delivery commitments.

Judge the brief by whether it helps the team make the next decision. Count missing blockers and unsupported completion claims. Ask reviewers whether they can inspect the source quickly. A concise summary is useful when its compression preserves the information that changes what someone should do.

6. Prepare customer onboarding check-ins

Trigger: a customer reaches a planned onboarding review point. Context: the agreed plan, approved progress notes, and unresolved questions. Output: a status recap and a draft check-in focused on the next required step.

A customer might have completed setup but still be waiting for an internal colleague to supply information. The proposed message should acknowledge what is done, identify the dependency, and make one clear request. It should avoid restarting the entire onboarding sequence or implying that a delayed step is the customer's fault.

The onboarding owner reviews the message and confirms the recipient. Account changes, subscription decisions, and promises about implementation support remain outside the initial workflow. Those actions may have different owners and should not be bundled into a routine check-in.

Measure whether the drafted message reflects the actual stage of the relationship. Look for repeated questions, outdated tasks, and unnecessary reminders. The goal is a more relevant next conversation. Any improvement in response or completion rates should be measured during a pilot rather than assumed in advance.

7. Turn recurring questions into knowledge drafts

Trigger: a team reviews a set of approved support or internal conversations. Context: those conversations and the current knowledge base. Output: proposed article topics, supporting examples, and a draft answer for an editor to assess.

Repeated questions about a setup step can reveal a missing explanation. Ask the agent to group the questions by underlying need and compare them with existing guidance. A cluster may call for a short clarification in an existing article rather than a completely new document.

Keep sensitive or identifying customer details out of proposed public examples. Give the editor the source references separately so the explanation can be checked without publishing private context. Require a subject-matter owner to approve product instructions and policy statements before publication.

Evaluate whether the suggested article answers a recurring question and whether its steps are accurate. A large number of topic suggestions is not the goal. A small number of useful, maintained explanations can be easier for a team to review and keep current.

Choose your first Claude agents with innflow pilot

Compare candidates on three practical questions: how often the task occurs, how easy its output is to review, and what happens when it is wrong. A recurring preparation task with an obvious reviewer is often a good first choice. Start there before connecting a long sequence of actions.

Choose a representative sample that includes ordinary requests and exceptions. Include short messages, incomplete context, conflicting dates, and requests outside the intended scope. Write down the expected response to each before running the agent. This gives you an acceptance test instead of a retrospective impression.

For a support-reply pilot, an example acceptance rule could require the draft to address the customer's question, cite the approved explanation, and avoid unsupported commitments. For a meeting recap, the rule could require every assigned owner and deadline to be present in the source notes.

Use review comments to improve the task instructions. If several reviewers repeatedly correct the same omission, add a clear requirement and rerun the affected examples. Keep previous results so the team can see whether the change helped or simply moved the error somewhere else.

Design the review and completion steps

Claude agents with innflow should be evaluated as complete workflows. Specify who receives the output, how they approve or revise it, and what records the final action. A draft in a queue and a message delivered to a customer are different outcomes. Name the one you are measuring.

For an external message, show the proposed recipient and content together. For a record update, show the existing value and the proposed change. For a task assignment, show the owner and the evidence for the request. Concrete review makes it easier to catch errors before they affect someone else.

Decide what happens after a failure. If a destination is unavailable, the result should remain visible with an owner and a retry decision. If the source is incomplete, the workflow should ask for the missing information. If the request exceeds its scope, it should route to a teammate who can decide.

When implementing Claude agents with innflow, verify those behaviors in the connected environment. A design diagram or an authenticated account does not prove that the final action works. Run an authorized test from input through review to completion, and inspect the record created at the destination.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are these ready-made innflow templates?

No. These are proposed workflow designs. Confirm the available model connection, tools, and actions in your workspace. Use the examples to define a pilot with your team, then validate the required connections before depending on them.

Do these workflows require the newest Claude model?

No particular model version is required by the design patterns. Choose a model available through your deployment and evaluate it against the actual task. More demanding preparation work may justify a different configuration from a short classification task.

What information should an agent receive?

Provide the information needed for its assigned task, including the relevant source records and current instructions. Define what happens when that context is unavailable. Avoid asking the agent to fill missing business facts from general knowledge.

How do we measure whether a pilot is useful?

Track accepted outputs, material corrections, review time, completion failures, and cost. Compare those results with the existing process. Review examples where the agent declined or escalated as well as examples it completed, because both affect the team's workload.

When should we allow more actions?

Expand only after the existing task performs acceptably on representative work and the next action has a clear owner, permission boundary, and completion check. Add one action at a time so problems can be located and corrected without disrupting the entire process.

Start with a useful handoff

The strongest first use case is one your team already understands. Pick a request that creates repetitive preparation work, define a useful result, and make review straightforward. Give the agent the context it needs, then judge its contribution by what the next person can do with the output.

That creates a practical foundation for Claude agents with innflow. You will know which steps are reliable, where human judgment adds value, and what the next integration needs to accomplish. The workflow can grow as the evidence improves.

Get started with innflow and bring one real workflow: the source conversation, the expected result, and the teammate responsible for the next step.

# 8 Use Cases for Grok Bot and Innflow: AI Teammates Plus Agent Workflows

SpaceXAI's Grok Bot is built around a simple idea. Instead of prompting an agent, you give work to a teammate. Each Bot runs on a persistent cloud computer with a browser, a filesystem, and a terminal. It can sign into the tools you already use, work across apps and websites (including ones without a clean API), and keep going while your laptop is closed. It only comes back to you when something needs your approval.

Bots can also work together. Several Bots share one computer, run in parallel, message each other, and coordinate in group chats. Recurring work becomes repeatable with two building blocks: a skill, which captures how a task is done, and a routine, which tells a Bot when to run it on a schedule or after an event such as a Slack message, a GitHub notification, or a webhook call.

Innflow is a general agent builder for workflow automation. You design agents that take in requests, follow your rules, connect to your tools, and keep a human in the loop where it matters.

The two fit together naturally. Innflow agents are a great way to run the structured, repeatable workflows your customers and team touch every day. Grok Bot teammates are a great way to handle the messy, cross-app work that happens around them. Here are eight ways to combine them.

## 1. Kick off a Grok Bot routine from an Innflow workflow

Grok Bot routines can be triggered by a webhook. When a routine has a webhook, a POST request starts a run, and a 200 response means the run started. That gives Innflow a clean handoff point. When an Innflow workflow reaches a step that needs hands-on work, such as researching an account across several sites or updating a portal with no API, it can call the routine's webhook and let the Bot take it from there.

## 2. Customer-facing intake, internal follow-through

Let an Innflow agent handle the front door: a form, a chat, or an inbound email. It qualifies the request and collects the details. Then a Grok Bot teammate picks up the internal side, like preparing the proposal, updating the CRM, and drafting the reply for your approval. Your customer gets a fast response, and your team gets finished work instead of a raw ticket.

## 3. Sales research and outreach prep

SpaceXAI describes Grok Bot handling sales outreach and marketing work. Pair that with an Innflow lead workflow. Innflow scores and routes inbound leads, and a Bot does the deeper research across LinkedIn, company sites, and your CRM, then drafts a personalized first message for you to review before anything goes out.

## 4. Content pipelines with an approval gate

Content teams juggle a calendar, drafts, images, and publishing. An Innflow workflow can own the structured part, moving a post from idea to draft to review with clear status rules. Grok Bot teammates can handle the cross-tool work around it, like pulling sources, updating the calendar, and preparing assets. Grok Bot's own guidance is to require approval before publishing, so the final push stays with a person.

## 5. Operations reporting on a schedule

A routine can run every weekday morning while you sleep. Have a Bot pull numbers from the dashboards you already use and post a short summary to Slack. Use Innflow for the workflows those numbers trigger, like alerting the right owner when a metric crosses a threshold or opening a task when something looks off.

## 6. Support escalations that arrive ready to act on

An Innflow support agent can resolve the common questions and apply your policies. When a case needs more digging, it hands off with a full summary. A Grok Bot teammate can then investigate across your inbox, billing tool, and internal docs, and come back with a recommended fix for a human to approve.

## 7. Learn it once, run it forever

Grok Bot can learn a workflow by following along while you do it once. It saves the steps and can rerun them on a schedule or on demand. Use that for the odd jobs your Innflow workflows depend on, like exporting a report from a legacy tool or updating a supplier portal, so the automation chain has no manual gaps.

## 8. A small team of specialists with one manager

SpaceXAI suggests running a chief of staff Bot on top of specialists for each lane, such as inbox, expenses, recruiting, or operations. Innflow agents slot in as the customer-facing and product-side workflows, while the Bots coordinate the internal work in group chats. You stop being the middleman passing context between tools.

## Designing it for trust

Grok Bot's documentation lays out good habits for routines, and they apply to the whole setup.

- Prepare before you execute. Have agents draft, reconcile, or recommend first.
- Gate the risky steps. Require approval for sending, purchasing, deleting, publishing, or changing production systems.
- Plan for missing data. Decide what happens when there is nothing new or the data is stale.
- Make retries safe. A workflow that runs twice should not send twice.
- Test after changes. Re-test when a website, connector, or data format changes.

## The takeaway

Grok Bot gives you AI teammates that can work across any app on their own computer, around the clock. Innflow gives you agent workflows with clear rules, triggers, and handoffs. Together, the structured work runs itself, and the messy work around it gets picked up by a teammate instead of landing back on your plate.

If you want to build the workflow side today, you can start designing agents in Innflow and connect them to the tools your team already uses.

Sources: SpaceXAI, "Introducing Grok Bot"; Grok Bot documentation (overview, and skills and routines); Grok Bot routines help.

# 7 Use Cases for Meta Muse and Innflow: Real-Time Avatars Backed by Agent Workflows

On September 23, 2026, Meta introduced Muse Realtime Avatar, a system that turns Muse Realtime Voice into an expressive, interactive avatar. A photo, an illustration, even an animal or an everyday object can become a character that talks, reacts, and gestures in a live conversation.

The numbers are what make it interesting for business use. Meta says Muse Realtime Avatar streams 448x768 portrait video at 25 frames per second with roughly 870 milliseconds from the end of a user's turn to the first byte of the synchronized voice and video reply. Voice and video are generated from the same stream of speech tokens, so lip motion and expression stay in sync with what is said. Every generated frame carries an invisible Meta Video Seal watermark so the output can be traced.

A live face is only half of a useful agent, though. The other half is what happens after the user asks for something: looking up a record, booking a slot, updating a CRM, filing a ticket, sending a follow-up. That is where Innflow comes in. Innflow is a general agent builder, so you can design the workflow an avatar hands off to, connect it to the tools your team already uses, and keep a human in the loop where it matters.

Here are seven ways to put the two together.

## 1. A live front desk for your website

Most website chat widgets feel like a form with a text box. A Muse style avatar can greet visitors, answer questions out loud, and keep the same look and mannerisms across the whole conversation. Behind it, an Innflow agent handles the real requests. It can check availability, qualify the lead with a few questions, and drop a meeting on the right calendar. The avatar talks. The workflow does the work.

## 2. Customer support that can actually resolve the ticket

A friendly face that can only say "I will pass this along" is not much of an upgrade. Pair the avatar with an Innflow support agent that can look up an order, check status in your system, apply the policy you define, and open or update a ticket. When the case needs a person, the agent routes it with a clean summary so nobody asks the customer to repeat themselves.

## 3. Onboarding and product walkthroughs

New users drop off when setup feels like homework. A live avatar can walk someone through the first steps, answer questions as they come up, and adjust the pace to the person in front of it. The Innflow side tracks which steps are complete, triggers the right welcome emails, and flags accounts that stall so your team can reach out.

## 4. Sales demos and lead qualification around the clock

Not every prospect books a call during business hours. An avatar can run a short, conversational discovery session at any time, and an Innflow agent can score the answers, enrich the contact, write the notes into your CRM, and book a follow-up with the right rep. Your team starts the next morning with qualified conversations instead of a pile of form fills.

## 5. Internal training and role-play

Muse can bring any character to life, which makes it a natural fit for practice. Picture a new hire rehearsing a tough customer call with an avatar that stays in character from turn to turn. Innflow can pull the scenario from your playbook, log each session, and send a short summary with coaching notes to the manager.

## 6. Branded characters for content and community

Brands already use mascots and personas. With a real-time avatar, that character can host a live Q and A, answer community questions, or front a product launch. An Innflow workflow can collect the questions ahead of time, pull approved answers from your knowledge base, and log anything new for the team to review afterward.

## 7. Accessible, voice-first self-service

Some people would rather talk than type, and a face that speaks can make a service feel more approachable. An avatar front end with an Innflow agent behind it lets someone ask for what they need in plain speech, like rescheduling an appointment, checking a balance, or requesting a document, while the workflow handles the steps and confirms the result.

## What to get right before you launch

A realistic avatar raises the bar on trust, so build a few guardrails in from day one.

- Be clear that it is AI. Tell people they are talking to an AI agent. Meta's watermarking helps with traceability, but the disclosure should be obvious in the experience itself.
- Keep actions behind rules. Let the avatar handle the conversation and let the Innflow workflow decide what is allowed, with approvals for anything sensitive like refunds or account changes.
- Hand off gracefully. Define when the agent should bring in a person, and pass along the full context when it does.
- Respect age and consent limits. Meta notes that the Muse app is for users aged 18 and older. Check the terms for any avatar service you use.

## The takeaway

Muse Realtime Avatar shows how quickly live AI presence is improving, with subsecond responses and expressions that stay consistent across a whole conversation. On its own, that is a better way to talk to an AI. Connected to Innflow agents, it becomes a better way to get something done: the avatar holds the conversation, and the workflow books the meeting, resolves the ticket, or updates the record.

If you want to design the workflow side today, you can start building agents in Innflow and connect them to the tools you already use.

Source: Meta AI Research, "Bringing Your Muse to Life," September 23, 2026.

properties.draft_blog:
Claude Opus 5.5 gives teams another reason to revisit the work they delegate to AI. A model upgrade can affect the quality of a proposed change, the time a reviewer spends checking it, and the cost of completing a task. Those differences matter when an agent handles a queue of real requests rather than a single demonstration.

Anthropic announced the model on September 22, 2026. This article covers the release facts first, then offers an evaluation approach for teams deciding whether to introduce it into their workflows. The examples below are proposed tests, not customer results or promises about what a deployment will achieve.

For a team with an existing process, the useful starting point is a task that already has a clear finish: a reviewed customer reply, an accurate meeting recap, or a code change that passes its checks. Use the new model to attempt the same work, keep the acceptance criteria stable, and examine what changed.

The Claude Opus 5.5 announcement at a glance

According to Anthropic's release announcement, the model is the first member of the Claude 5.5 family. Anthropic reports improvements in coding, communication, and its behavioral safety evaluations. It lists standard API pricing at $4 per million input tokens, $20 per million output tokens, and $0.20 per million cache-read tokens. The company estimates 40% lower costs than Opus 5 on typical workloads at default settings. That estimate is a vendor test result, not a guaranteed reduction for an individual workflow.

Anthropic lists availability through the Claude Platform and major cloud providers, with the API identifier claude-opus-5-5. Its announcement says Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 will follow. Check the provider you use for account access, regional availability, and current pricing before planning a rollout. These release details were checked on September 28, 2026.

What a model upgrade changes inside an agent

An agent's output depends on more than its model. It needs a task, relevant context, access to appropriate tools, and a way to tell whether the task is finished. Changing the model affects one part of that system. It does not automatically repair an outdated knowledge base, an unclear instruction, or a connection that cannot reach the required record.

Anthropic's tool-use documentation describes how Claude can request structured tool calls. With client tools, the surrounding application executes the call and returns a result. This separation matters: a proposed action and a successfully completed action are distinct events.

Consider an agent preparing a customer follow-up. It may read an approved conversation, identify an unanswered question, and produce a useful draft. The workflow still needs to identify the correct customer, choose the destination, and obtain any required review. If the send fails, the system should report that failure rather than treating a well-written draft as completed outreach.

When evaluating Claude Opus 5.5, examine the transitions between those steps. Does the agent recognize missing information? Does it use the information it retrieved? Does its final message distinguish work it prepared from work it completed? These observations often give an operations team more useful evidence than a broad impression that the new model sounds better.

Choose tests that resemble your team's actual work

Start with context-heavy preparation

A good initial task requires reading and organizing information but has a result that a teammate can check quickly. For example, ask the agent to prepare a project handoff from an approved set of notes. Require it to identify the objective, decisions, unresolved questions, and next owner. Include links back to the evidence for each material statement.

Introduce realistic complications. One note may describe an old deadline while a later note changes it. Two people may disagree about the next step. A task may lack an owner. The desired behavior is to preserve that uncertainty and make review easier. A polished document that silently fills those gaps should fail the test.

Include bounded implementation work

For a development team, choose a small issue with an observable outcome. Give the agent the repository instructions, the expected behavior, and the relevant checks. Ask for a change and an explanation of what was verified. Keep the review focused on the resulting behavior, the scope of the diff, and any untested assumptions.

A useful comparison includes an ordinary case and an exception. The ordinary case shows whether the model can finish the work. The exception shows whether it can stop appropriately when the requested behavior conflicts with an existing constraint. Both belong in the same evaluation, because production queues contain both.

Test the handoff as carefully as the answer

Give the reviewer a consistent output format: result, supporting evidence, proposed next action, and open questions. Then ask whether another teammate could continue without rereading the entire source material. If the handoff forces the reviewer to reconstruct the task, record that as additional work even when the underlying answer is correct.

This test is especially useful across departments. Sales, support, engineering, and operations may describe the same request differently. A good handoff should preserve the customer's request while translating it into a next step the receiving team can act on. Define what that translation means before comparing model outputs.

Evaluate cost per accepted result

Token prices help estimate a budget, but they do not capture the complete cost of a workflow. An agent can consume fewer tokens and still create more work if its result needs extensive correction. Another run can cost more at the model layer while saving a reviewer time. Measure both parts rather than choosing one in isolation.

A practical evaluation record can include input size, output size, tool calls, retries, elapsed time, and reviewer minutes. Add a simple acceptance decision and the reason for rejection when a result fails. This makes it possible to distinguish expensive but useful work from cheap output that never becomes a completed task.

As a hypothetical example, imagine a recap task that finishes quickly but assigns a commitment to the wrong person. The reviewer corrects the owner and checks every other assignment. Count that correction time. Do not classify the result as fully successful simply because the model produced all the requested headings.

For Claude Opus 5.5, run the same representative tasks under the settings you intend to use. Record the model identifier and configuration with the results. Avoid comparing one model's carefully tuned run with another model's default setup and then treating the difference as a universal performance ranking.

Budget for exceptions as well. If a tool is unavailable, the agent may need to stop, retry, or ask for help. Those paths consume time even when the model behaves correctly. A reliable cost estimate includes how often the workflow reaches them and who handles the remaining work.

Build a migration decision around evidence

Use a written scorecard before running the comparison. A compact scorecard might ask whether the result is factually supported, complete for the stated task, correctly scoped, and easy to review. Give critical errors their own category. A mistaken recipient should not disappear inside an otherwise strong average score.

Keep source material and instructions consistent across candidates. Where possible, hide the model name from reviewers so they judge the work without expectations about the release. Run more than one example from each important task category. One excellent response is useful evidence, but it is too narrow to justify changing an entire queue.

Record disagreement between reviewers. If two knowledgeable teammates cannot agree whether an answer is acceptable, the workflow may need clearer criteria. Resolve that ambiguity before trying to solve it through prompt changes. The evaluation should improve the definition of the work as well as your understanding of the model.

Finish with a specific decision for each task. You might adopt the model for drafting complex handoffs, retain another configuration for simple extraction, and defer actions that need additional controls. A mixed decision is reasonable when the tasks have different costs, consequences, and review requirements.

A practical rollout plan for Claude Opus 5.5

  1. Define one outcome. Name the input, expected result, owner, and completion check. Keep the first workflow small enough to inspect from beginning to end.
  2. Capture a baseline. Measure the existing process using representative cases. Include rejected results and manual corrections, not just successful examples.
  3. Run a preparation-only trial. Let the agent produce drafts or recommendations while a teammate performs the consequential action. Review the evidence attached to each result.
  4. Exercise failure paths. Try missing context, conflicting instructions, unavailable tools, and interrupted runs. Confirm that the workflow leaves a clear next step.
  5. Expand one permission at a time. Add an action only after its inputs, approval rules, and completion signal are understood. Keep a way to return to the prior configuration.

Choose a named owner for the trial. That person should be able to inspect failures, change instructions, and decide whether to pause the workflow. Ownership prevents a common operational problem: everyone can see that something went wrong, but no one is responsible for resolving the queue.

Document changes during the pilot. If you update a prompt, connector, or knowledge source, record it beside the model configuration. Otherwise, an apparent improvement can be attributed to the wrong cause. Clear change records also make it easier to reproduce a successful setup later.

The approval boundary should be visible in the work itself. A reviewer should see what is proposed, which records it affects, and what evidence supports it. Avoid asking for a generic approval that covers an unspecified sequence of future actions. Specific review is easier to perform and easier to audit.

Where innflow fits in the evaluation

innflow describes a workflow centered on connected conversations, focused agent tasks, relevant context, and team review. That provides a useful starting point for evaluating a new model: choose a real request, define the next step, and make the result understandable to the person responsible for it.

For a proposed customer-follow-up pilot, begin with a small set of approved conversations. Define the output as a summary and an unsent reply. Require the agent to surface unanswered questions and avoid inventing commitments. Let the account owner decide whether the draft is ready to send.

For an internal operations pilot, use a recurring handoff between two teams. Specify what the receiving team needs and which information the agent can read. Evaluate whether the prepared handoff reduces repeated questions. Keep the source record available so that disagreements can be resolved against the evidence.

Confirm model availability and the required integrations in your actual innflow workspace before implementing either example. This article does not establish that a particular model version or connector is enabled for every account. A model announcement is a reason to evaluate a workflow; the result of that evaluation should determine the deployment.

Frequently Asked Questions

When was Claude Opus 5.5 announced?

Anthropic announced it on September 22, 2026. The official release page is linked above. This draft reflects information checked on September 28, so verify current access and commercial terms again when implementing the model.

Does a newer model mean an existing agent will work better?

It is a reason to test, not an acceptance result. Run the new model against your existing task criteria and inspect accuracy, completion, review effort, and cost. Keep failures visible rather than evaluating only the most impressive examples.

What should a small team test first?

Choose a recurring preparation task with accessible evidence and a clear reviewer. Meeting recaps, request summaries, and internal handoffs are useful candidates. Start where a person can recognize a correct result without doing the entire task again.

Can the model complete actions without review?

That depends on the surrounding application, tool access, and authorization rules. Decide permissions at the workflow level. Begin with narrow actions and explicit completion checks, and keep consequential decisions with the person responsible for them.

How should teams decide whether to migrate?

Compare accepted outcomes on representative work. Include correction time, operational failures, and the effort needed to maintain the setup. Adopt the configuration that meets your requirements for the specific task, then keep measuring it as those requirements change.

Turn the announcement into a focused experiment

The useful next step is a small, observable trial. Give the model a task with a clear finish, provide the context it needs, and evaluate the result against the same criteria your team already uses. Record both the successful work and the cases that require intervention.

That approach gives you a concrete migration decision. You can explain what improved, what remained difficult, and which actions still require review. It also creates a reusable evaluation process for the next release, so each new announcement becomes easier to assess.

Ready to connect a focused agent task to your team's work? Get started with innflow and define the request, expected output, and review point for your first pilot.
