properties.draft_blog:
PayProp is a payments machine. Do not review it like a full PMS

Most software writeups flatten every vendor into the same feature grid: accounting, leasing, maintenance, owner portal, mobile app. PayProp does not sit in the center of that grid. It is built around rent collection, reconciliation, trust-style client money handling, and automated payouts. If you score it as if it were AppFolio or Buildium, you will call it incomplete. If you score it as a payment operations layer, the review gets honest.

This article covers PayProp reviews pricing features and alternatives the way an operator should: what the product actually does, where reviewers praise it, where they stall, how pricing is sold, and which alternatives make sense by job to be done. innflow is not a PayProp clone and not a property management system of record. It is the AI agent and workflow layer you put on top when the money system still leaves human queues behind.

Confirm current packaging on a live demo. Payment products change fee schedules and regional banking partners. Nothing here is an offer or a fee quote.

What PayProp is in 2026

PayProp markets itself as rental property management software with a payment-first spine. The US site emphasizes automated rent collection, real-time reconciliation, trust accounts with accurate totals, arrears reminders, maintenance tickets, and integrations. The company has a longer history in the UK and other markets as a lettings-payment platform, which shows up in the product’s bias: money movement and client accounting first, CRM second.

That bias is the buying criterion. A third-party manager drowning in owner statements, contractor bills, and commission splits will care more about settlement rules than about a pretty listing syndicator. A mom-and-pop landlord who needs applications, e-signatures, and a maintenance marketplace may find the rest of the stack thin.

Typical buyer: a small to midsize residential operator, often a third-party manager, who wants rent in, fees taken, owners and vendors paid, and arrears visible without a bookkeeper rebuilding every batch. Less typical buyer: a large multifamily shop that already lives in an enterprise PMS and only needs a processor. Those teams should ask whether PayProp is a system of record or a payments companion. Mixing those jobs without a plan creates dual ledgers.

PayProp features that matter in a review

Ignore brochure adjectives. Review the jobs.

Incoming rent and reconciliation

This is the core. PayProp is designed to take resident payments and match them without a Friday export ritual. Reviewers who like the product almost always start here: less manual allocation, fewer “where did this deposit come from” tickets, faster month-end. If your current pain is a lockbox file and a highlighter, this is the feature that can change the week.

In a demo, watch a messy payment, not a perfect one. Ask what happens to a short pay, a double pay, a payment with no unit number, and an ACH that returns after you already showed the owner a paid ledger.

Automated trust-style accounting and outgoing payments

PayProp’s differentiator is rule-based money out. Management fees, landlord payouts, and contractor bills can be calculated and sent from the same flow that took the rent in. For managers, that is the product. For owner-operators who pay themselves from one account, it is less magical.

Ask how rules are versioned when a management fee changes mid-tenancy. Ask how the system handles a repair that should be paid before the owner draw. Ask what the owner statement looks like to a non-accountant. User reviews have flagged statements that take time to learn, especially on more complex block or multi-owner setups.

Arrears management

Live arrears views plus text and email reminders are table stakes, and PayProp treats them as part of the payment spine rather than a separate collections product. That is useful if your delinquency process is currently a spreadsheet. It is not a legal collections suite. You still need notice templates, state rules, and a human gate before anything that looks like a threat to housing.

Tenant records, vacancies, expenses, and maintenance

PayProp includes tenant tracking (lease dates, payments, late fees), vacancy tracking, expense tools, and maintenance tickets from the dashboard. Treat these as supporting modules. They can be enough for a lean shop. They are not the reason to pick PayProp over a full PMS if leasing CRM, inspection tools, or owner portals are the bottleneck.

Integrations and access

The vendor highlights connections to accounting, marketing, and inspection tools, plus an API. Remote and multi-device access is a consistent plus in reviews. Integration quality varies by market and by which general ledger you actually run. Do not take “we integrate” as “your chart of accounts will map in a day.”

PayProp pricing: what you can know without a quote

PayProp does not publish a simple public rate card for US operators the way some per-unit PMS vendors do. Pricing is typically delivered through a demo and a proposal. Some third-party directories show a low monthly starting point, but directory numbers go stale and often omit payment fees, payout fees, and implementation.

When you request a quote, force the proposal into a total cost of collection:

  • Platform or per-unit software fee
  • ACH and card processing, including who pays card convenience fees
  • Return, chargeback, and exception fees
  • Owner and vendor payout costs
  • Onboarding, training, and any banking or trust setup
  • Contract term. The vendor advertises no long-term contracts in some markets. Get that in the order form.

A free demo and product tour are available. Use them to time a real close cycle, not to watch a happy-path video. Affordability comments in reviews are generally favorable relative to heavier PMS suites, which makes sense if you are buying a payments engine rather than a 40-module platform. Cheap becomes expensive if you still need a second system for leasing and accounting depth.

What reviewers get right: pros and cons

Strengths

  • Payment automation is the point, not an add-on. Rent in, rules applied, money out is a coherent design.
  • Reconciliation labor can drop. Teams that lived in bank files notice this first.
  • Client-money confidence is a first-class story, which matters for licensed managers.
  • Arrears visibility is built into the same object as the payment, not a bolted-on aging report.
  • Support is polarizing but often praised when onboarding is staffed well. Some users report a smooth start.

Weaknesses

  • Statements and reports can be hard to learn. If your owners want a one-page cash snapshot, budget time to design that view or export it.
  • Setup is not instant. Bank connections, rules, and historical balances take real project hours.
  • Support response is uneven in some reviews. Payment systems cannot afford a slow ticket on a failed payout week. Ask for support hours and escalation paths in the demo.
  • Broader property operations are thinner than a full PMS: marketing, screening depth, inspections, and portfolio analytics may need other tools.
  • Dual-system risk. If you keep another ledger, you now have two truths. Decide which system owns cash before you go live.

Who should buy PayProp, and who should not

Buy PayProp when the bottleneck is money movement: late posting, messy owner draws, manual commission splits, and arrears that nobody sees until month-end. It fits managers who will accept a payment-centric system of record, or who have a clear integration plan into an existing general ledger.

Do not buy PayProp as a magic replacement for a leasing-heavy or enterprise multifamily stack. If your pain is make-ready cycle time, ILS posting, affordable housing compliance, or a 200-report owner packet, look at a full PMS and keep a processor decision separate.

Also pause if your team cannot name a single payments process owner. Software will not invent one. Shared ownership of trust rules is how you get two fee schedules and a surprise clawback.

Alternatives, by job to be done

Compare alternatives to the job, not to a logo wall. innflow is listed last on purpose: it is orchestration, not a PayProp replacement.

Full property management suites

Buildium, AppFolio, Rent Manager, and similar platforms put leasing, accounting, maintenance, and portals in one product. Choose these when you need a system of record for the whole operation and are willing to take their native payments. You will usually pay more per unit and spend more on implementation. You may get a weaker payments rule engine than a specialist. That trade can still be correct.

Accounting-forward or payment-forward PMS tools

Propertyware and other accounting-heavy products compete more directly with PayProp’s money story. Expect per-unit pricing with monthly minimums on some of these. Innago and other lighter tools compete on low software price and then make it up in payment fees. Model the fee mix. A “free” platform with expensive rails can cost more than a quoted PayProp book.

Stand-alone processors plus your current PMS

If your PMS is fine and only collections are ugly, a dedicated processor or lockbox upgrade can be enough. This is often cheaper than a rip-and-replace. It fails when the PMS cannot post cleanly or when owner disbursement still lives in a spreadsheet.

innflow on top of whatever you keep

If the system of record is staying, the remaining work is still real: failed-payment chase, arrears notices, owner questions, unmatched cash, vendor bills waiting on approval. That is workflow work. innflow runs those multi-step flows across tools. It does not hold trust funds and does not pretend to be your ledger.

How to run a PayProp evaluation without getting sold a tour

Name a process owner for the evaluation. Give them four weeks, not a single webinar.

  1. Write the current money path: who posts rent, who handles returns, who pays owners, who pays vendors, what the SLA is.
  2. Export 30 days of exceptions: NSF, misapplied cash, owner complaints about statements, late vendor bills.
  3. In the demo, replay those exceptions. Happy-path rent is not a test.
  4. Price total cost of collection on your ACH/card mix.
  5. Decide the system of record for cash before you sign.
  6. Pilot one entity or one market through a full billing cycle.
  7. Only then move the rest of the book.

Keep human gates on refunds, hardship plans, and anything that changes an owner’s money. Automate posting, reminders, and rule-based splits once those gates are explicit.

How innflow fits next to PayProp

innflow is the AI agent and workflow automation platform built for real work. Agents connect to tools, run multi-step flows, and keep execution visible on a canvas. They are not a payments processor and not a chatbot with a rent theme.

Beside PayProp, or beside any payment-first PMS, innflow is useful when:

  • A failed payment needs a structured ticket, a first notice, and an escalation, not a hope that the resident opens the portal.
  • Arrears work has to include lease context, prior notices, and a legal-review gate.
  • Owner questions about a payout need a packaged answer from the ledger and the rule that fired.
  • Maintenance invoices sit between “approved” and “paid” with no owner.
  • You run PayProp plus another system and need a visible handoff instead of a private spreadsheet.

Keep PayProp (or your chosen PMS) as the cash system of record. Use innflow to orchestrate the human and multi-tool work around that record. Start with one path: returned payments or unmatched deposits. Measure cycle time to resolved ledger. Expand after a full operating cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is PayProp a full property management system?

It includes tenant, vacancy, expense, and maintenance tools, but its center of gravity is payments and client accounting. If you need a deep leasing CRM or enterprise multifamily suite, treat PayProp as a specialist and compare it that way.

How much does PayProp cost?

US pricing is quote-based. Ask for software fees and payment fees on one page, using your real volume. Directory “starting at” numbers are not a budget.

What do PayProp reviews complain about most?

The recurring themes are statement complexity, a long setup, and uneven support response. The recurring praise is automated collection and less reconciliation work. Both can be true in the same shop if onboarding is understaffed.

Should we replace our PMS with PayProp?

Only if payments and owner disbursement are the binding constraint and you are willing to make PayProp the cash system of record. If leasing and maintenance are the constraint, keep the PMS and fix processing separately.

Where does innflow belong in this decision?

innflow does not replace PayProp. It orchestrates the exception and communication workflows that still sit around any payments platform: intake, SLAs, handoffs, and visible status.

Conclusion

PayProp is strongest where rent has to move, match, and pay out under rules a manager can repeat. Review it on that job. Price the whole collection stack, test ugly payments, and decide which system owns cash. If you need a broader operating system, pick a full PMS. If you need the work around payments to stop living in inboxes, add orchestration rather than another ledger.

When you are ready to run those exception flows with agents you can inspect, deploy with innflow. Get Started at app.innflow.ai, or Talk to Sales at innflow.ai.

Online rent is not a button. It is a collection system residents will actually finish

Offering a pay link is easy. Collecting rent on the first of the month, posting it to the right unit, and knowing what to do when the draft fails is the job. Teams that “turned on online payments” still chase screenshots, still take hallway cash, and still discover on the fifth that half the book never enrolled in autopay.

This is a practical guide to online rent payments how accept them and how to run collection after the portal is live. It covers the resident path, the rails that belong in a rental book, enrollment tactics, reminder cadence, partial payments, and the delinquency handoff. It is adjacent to payment processing, but the focus here is collection behavior, not merchant-account contracts. Confirm late-fee and notice rules with counsel in each state. This is not legal advice.

innflow belongs on the follow-up spine: enrollment gaps, failed drafts, reminder SLAs, and a packaged handoff into formal collections. It does not replace your portal or your processor.

Why online collection is an operating standard in 2026

Residents already pay everything else from a phone. A paper-only shop is not traditional. It is slow, and it hides delinquency until the lockbox file lands. Online payments give you a timestamp, a method, a receipt, and a failure code. That is the raw material of a collection process.

The 2026 version of the problem is not “should we accept online rent.” It is adoption and exception design. You can have a portal and still have:

  • A third of residents who never set up a payment method
  • Autopay that dies when a debit card expires
  • Roommates who each paid half to the wrong ledger
  • Staff who accept unofficial apps and then cannot reverse a dispute
  • Late fees that post on different days in different regions

Online collection only works when the official path is easier than the unofficial one, and when every failure creates work with an owner. Convenience without a workflow is just a prettier way to be late.

How to accept online rent: the resident path

Build one official path. Publish it in the lease, the move-in packet, the portal, and the first live conversation. Then refuse to invent a second path in the hallway.

1. Issue credentials before keys, not after the first due date

Create the resident user, the recurring charge, and the autopay invitation as part of move-in. If credentials go out on the 28th for a lease that started on the 1st, you trained them to pay some other way. Walk the resident through a test login. Do not assume an email arrived.

2. Offer ACH as the default rail

Bank draft is the workhorse for recurring rent. It is usually cheaper than cards and cleaner for autopay. Collect authorization in the portal, store the mandate, and label it on the ledger. Make card pay available if you want last-minute conversion, but do not let cards become the silent default because the ACH form has too many fields.

3. Turn on autopay with a confirmation the resident can see

Autopay is the collection product. One-time pay is the backup. Show the draft date, the amount logic (base rent plus recurring charges), and what happens if the balance changes. Residents cancel autopay when a surprise charge hits. Predictable drafts keep the mandate alive.

4. Send a receipt that matches the ledger

The receipt should show property, unit, amount, method, confirmation number, and remaining balance. A processor email that says “Thank you for your payment” with no unit number is how roommate disputes start. If you accept a payment, the resident should be able to prove what it covered.

5. Close unofficial channels

If a resident can Venmo a superintendent and get a thumbs-up, your portal is optional. Write a one-line policy: unofficial payments are not recognized until they are reversed into the official rail. Then back the staff who enforce it. Collection systems die from friendly exceptions.

Best practices that actually move on-time pay

Software does not collect rent. Cadence, clarity, and consequences do. Use the portal as the channel, not as the strategy.

Publish the calendar

Residents should know, without asking, when rent is due, when reminders go out, when late fees post, and when a formal notice starts. Put that calendar in the lease and in the portal. If your markets have different grace periods, say so by property. A single national “we are flexible” sentence is how two managers invent two policies.

Remind before the due date, not only after

A useful reminder sequence is boring on purpose:

  • A few days before due: balance, due date, autopay status, official pay link
  • Due date: confirmation for those who paid, a short pay-now note for those who have not
  • After grace: late fee posted, remaining balance, official path only
  • After the notice threshold: handoff to the delinquency workflow, not another casual nudge

Do not send five brand-new messages from five people. One voice, one balance, one link. Extra chatter trains residents to ignore you.

Make enrollment a scored task

Track three adoption numbers: residents with a portal login, residents with a stored payment method, and residents on autopay. Login without a method is not adoption. Review the gaps weekly by property. Call or text the holdouts with a script, not a lecture. Offer a five-minute setup window at move-in and at renewal. After that, paper pay should be harder, not easier.

Decide partial payments in writing

If you accept partials, apply them in a published order and keep the remaining balance visible. If you do not accept them, reject them quickly so the resident cannot claim they “paid something.” Either rule can be right. An unwritten rule is how you waive your way into a bad habit.

Keep late fees mechanical

Late fees that depend on who answers the phone are not late fees. They are discounts. Post them when the lease says they are earned, allow documented waivers through one owner, and log the reason. Online payments make this easier because the timestamp is not a debate.

Treat failed autopay as day-zero work

A failed draft is not a reminder problem. It is a broken mandate or an empty account. Same-day notice, a retry rule that you can explain, and a switch to a good-funds method if the rail is dead. Endless silent retries look like harassment and still do not post rent.

The delinquency workflow after online pay fails

Online collection does not eliminate delinquency. It timestamps it. Design the path from “not paid” to “resolved or legal.”

  1. Detect: unpaid or failed payment after the cutoff, with method and amount.
  2. Notify: official balance and pay path, within an SLA measured in hours, not “when we get to it.”
  3. Qualify: is this a dead card, a dispute, a hardship request, or a skip?
  4. Plan or notice: either a written payment plan with dates, or the statutory notice your market requires.
  5. Gate: a human reviews anything that starts a legal clock or a plan that changes amounts.
  6. Close: paid, plan current, unit in legal, or skip/trace. No zombie balances in a side spreadsheet.

Name a process owner for collections. Site staff can have the first conversation. They should not invent terms. Package every exception with the ledger, the reminder history, and the last successful payment so the next person is not starting from zero.

Hardship is a real category. Treat it as an intake form: what is owed, what the resident can pay, what date, what proof. A story in the inbox is not a plan. If you offer a plan, pause conflicting late-fee automation so you do not look chaotic.

Compliance notes operators skip

Online payments sit next to several rules that are easy to trip over:

  • Late fees and grace periods are state and sometimes city specific. The portal must match the lease, not the vendor’s default.
  • Convenience fees on cards are restricted in some places. Do not toggle a surcharge because the processor UI allows it.
  • Fair debt communications still apply when you start sounding like a collector. Scripts should be reviewed.
  • Autopay authorization should be clear on amount, timing, and how to cancel.
  • Receipts and ledgers are your evidence in a dispute. If staff adjust balances off-system, you will lose that fight.

None of this requires you to become a lawyer. It does require one owner who can say “the portal setting is wrong” and have it changed the same week.

How innflow runs online collection after the portal exists

innflow is the AI agent and workflow automation platform built for real work. Agents connect to your portal, PMS, and inbox, run multi-step flows, and keep execution visible on a canvas. They are not a replacement chatbot for “where do I pay.” That answer should already be in the lease.

A practical innflow collection spine:

  • Flag residents who have keys but no stored payment method, and run an enrollment sequence with a human follow-up if they ignore it.
  • Watch for failed autopay and open a ticket with reason code, amount, and last good payment.
  • Send the pre-due and post-due reminders from one template set, then stop when a formal notice workflow starts so you do not double-message.
  • Route hardship replies into a structured intake and package them for the manager who can approve a plan.
  • Assemble the delinquency file (ledger, notices, payment attempts) when the SLA for informal collection expires.
  • Digest daily: unenrolled new move-ins, failed drafts, plans that missed a step, notices waiting on a signature.

Keep the portal and the PMS as systems of record. innflow orchestrates the work around them. Start with failed-draft intake plus new-resident enrollment. Those two paths are high volume and easy to score. Expand into formal notice packaging after the first paths hold for a full billing cycle.

A thirty-day standup for teams that already “have online pay”

If the portal exists and collection still feels manual, do not buy another button. Run this month:

  • Week 1: Export who is on autopay, who pays one-time, who still pays paper. Name the process owner.
  • Week 2: Fix move-in so credentials and autopay invites happen before keys. Kill unofficial pay channels in writing.
  • Week 3: Standardize the reminder calendar and the late-fee post time. Align portal settings to the lease.
  • Week 4: Automate failed-payment tickets in innflow. Review exception cycle time. Write down the three exceptions that still leak.

You will know it worked when staff stop asking “did they pay” and start asking “why is this exception still open.”

Frequently Asked Questions

Should we require online rent in the lease?

Require the official method, and make online the default. Some residents will still need a cash-equivalent path. Offer that path through a documented money order or kiosk, not through a manager’s personal account. Check local rules before you make electronic pay the only legal option.

Is autopay fair if charges change?

It is fair if you disclose that the draft equals the current balance or a stated set of recurring charges, and you notify residents when that set changes. Surprise drafts are how mandates die.

What if residents say the portal is too hard?

Watch one of them try it. If the form is actually bad, fix the form. If they never opened the email, the problem is enrollment, not UX. Sit with new residents at move-in and complete the first method together.

How is this different from choosing a payment processor?

The processor moves money. Online collection is the resident behavior and the desk that handles failure. You can have a fine processor and still fail collection if nobody owns reminders, enrollment, and plans.

Where should AI agents start?

Start with enrollment gaps and failed drafts. Leave legal notices and hardship approvals to humans with a full packet. innflow is built for that split: agents on the spine, people on the judgment.

Conclusion

Accepting online rent is the easy half. Collecting it is a designed path: credentials before keys, ACH and autopay as the default, one reminder voice, mechanical late fees, and a delinquency handoff that does not start from a blank inbox. If unofficial channels are easier than the portal, the portal will lose.

When you want that follow-up work to run with visible owners and SLAs, deploy with innflow. Get Started at app.innflow.ai, or Talk to Sales at innflow.ai.

properties.draft_blog:
On-Site is a small-portfolio PMS. Do not confuse it with enterprise OneSite

Search “On-Site property manager” and you will hit two different products in your head. One is RealPage OneSite, the heavy multifamily operating system used by large communities. The other is OnSite Property Manager (often styled On-Site), a web-based tool aimed at landlords and small managers who want rent charges, expenses, payments, move-in and move-out, and paperless work orders without an enterprise implementation.

This on-site property manager software review is about the second product. Reviewing it as if it were OneSite, Yardi, or AppFolio is how you write a useless comparison. Reviewing it as an affordable system of record for a small residential or mixed book is how you decide whether it is enough, or whether you have already outgrown it.

innflow is not an On-Site alternative. It does not keep the rent roll. It is the AI agent and workflow layer you add when the PMS stores records and the team still chases work in email. Confirm current plans and fees on the vendor site. Pricing pages move.

What On-Site Property Manager is in 2026

On-Site is a browser-based rental management product for residential and commercial doors. The pitch is access and simplicity: log in from any device, post charges, take online tenant payments, track bills, run a move-in or move-out, and send a work order without printing a three-part form.

That positioning tells you the buyer. An owner with a handful of units, or a small manager who is leaving spreadsheets, will care that the same feature set is available on the cheapest unit band. A regional multifamily operator will care that there is no deep leasing CRM, no institutional reporting pack, and no implementation army. Both observations can be true.

The product’s job is to be the ledger and the tenant file for a book that is still human-scale. If your book is no longer human-scale, stop reading the feature list and start reading the workflow gaps.

On-Site features, reviewed as work

Automatic charges

On-Site can calculate and post rent and late fees, plus other recurring charges such as utilities. Tenants get an email when a charge posts. For a small book, this is the difference between remembering the first of the month and actually billing the first of the month.

In a review, the question is control, not existence. Can you set late-fee rules that match each lease? Can you suppress a fee during a documented plan? Can you post a one-time charge without breaking the recurring schedule? If the answer is “email support and they will adjust it,” you do not have a charge engine. You have a help desk.

Expense tracking

Bills can be entered, scheduled, color-coded by status, and paid, including check printing from the browser. Invoices and receipts can be uploaded so owner and expense reports populate from the same record. This is useful when the alternative is a shoebox and a personal checking account.

It is less useful when you need true trust accounting, management-company books separate from owner books, or a close that an outside CPA will sign without reconstruction. Ask to see an owner statement and a property-level profit view on a property with mixed deposits and a vendor bill paid from the wrong entity. Pretty calendars do not fix a commingled account.

Move-in and move-out

The product handles the tenant lifecycle: prospect to current to past, prorated rent, starting balances, security deposits, and transfers between properties with a transfer charge. For operators who still move people on paper, this is real time saved.

Stress-test the messy cases. Mid-month move-in with prepaid rent. Roommate added after the fact. Transfer that should move a credit but not a late fee. Move-out where the deposit is held past the statutory deadline because someone forgot the clock. If those paths are manual, budget staff time. Lifecycle screens are only as good as the exceptions.

Online tenant payments

Residents can pay and view statements after the manager invites them by email. The processor deposits to the manager’s bank account and issues receipts. That is the minimum viable collection stack, and it is enough for many small portfolios.

Ask the fee question in writing: ACH versus card, who pays convenience fees, return fees, and how a payment posts when it later fails. A portal that says Paid while the bank says Returned will wreck your aging report. Also ask whether unofficial payments (personal apps, hallway cash) can be recorded without pretending they came through the processor.

Paperless work orders

Tenants submit a request with notes, photos, and documents. The vendor gets an email or text and a way to see status. For a 20-unit book, that can replace the group text that nobody owns.

It will not replace a maintenance operation. There is no serious dispatch board, no technician capacity view, no parts inventory, and no make-ready machine. If work orders are your bottleneck at 400 units, you are shopping in the wrong aisle.

On-Site pricing shape

On-Site sells unit-tiered monthly plans. The vendor publicly advertises a low starting price for the smallest band, historically in single-digit dollars per month for a handful of units, with a higher band for the next unit block. Feature access is the same across those early tiers. You pay for unit count, not for unlocking basic tools. There is a trial, and the vendor emphasizes no long contracts and unlimited users on published materials.

Treat published starting prices as a directional signal, not a budget. Confirm the current bands, what happens when you cross a unit threshold mid-month, and every payment processing fee that sits outside the software subscription. A cheap PMS with expensive card rails is not cheap.

The pricing story is the product story: this is meant to stay affordable while you are small. The moment you need implementation, training, custom reports, and a customer-success manager, you are no longer in the market this price was built for.

Pros, cons, and fit

Where On-Site is a fair buy

  • You are leaving spreadsheets or paper ledgers.
  • You want one login for charges, expenses, payments, and simple work orders.
  • You manage residential, small commercial, or a mix, and you do not need affordable-housing or enterprise modules.
  • Several people need access without paying a per-seat tax.
  • You will accept a web app and a lean report set.

Where On-Site is the wrong tool

  • You need institutional accounting, trust compliance depth, or a close that feeds a fund.
  • Leasing velocity depends on ILS posting, a CRM pipeline, and e-sign at volume.
  • Maintenance is a shop, not a handful of vendors.
  • Owners expect a branded portal and a packet that matches their investor report.
  • You already run another PMS and are only shopping because a blog compared logos.

User sentiment on lightweight tools like this is usually about ease versus ceiling. People praise that they can start quickly. They leave when the book grows and the exceptions no longer fit the screens. That is not a smear. It is the product doing what it advertised, then meeting a different company.

Alternatives, compared honestly

Do not replace On-Site with a random “best of” list. Match the job.

Stay on On-Site and add process

If the records are fine and the pain is follow-up (late rent, vendor no-shows, move-out clocks), buying a heavier PMS will recreate the same queues in a nicer UI. Fix the workflow first.

Move to a mid-market all-in-one

Buildium, AppFolio, Rent Manager, TenantCloud, and similar products cost more and cover more: deeper accounting, stronger portals, marketing, and more mature payment stacks. Choose them when you have outgrown unit-tier simplicity and can staff an implementation. You will pay in money and in change management.

Enterprise suites

Yardi, RealPage OneSite, Entrata, and peers are not On-Site alternatives in any serious sense. They are operating systems for large communities. If that is your world, you already know. Do not run a 12-unit test in OneSite because the names sound related.

Processor plus spreadsheets

Some owners only needed online pay. A stand-alone payment tool can be cheaper than any PMS. It fails as soon as you need a rent roll, a deposit register, and a work-order history in one place.

innflow as orchestration, not a PMS

innflow does not post rent or print checks. It runs the multi-step work around whatever system of record you keep: intake, routing, reminders, exception packets, visible handoffs. Use it when On-Site (or any PMS) stores the truth and people still carry the process in their heads.

How to evaluate On-Site in thirty days

Name a process owner for the evaluation. Shared shopping is how you buy a tool nobody runs.

  1. Write the current path for one charge cycle, one move-in, one work order, and one owner report.
  2. List the five exceptions that burned time last month.
  3. In the trial, replay those exceptions. Ignore the clean demo property.
  4. Price software plus payment fees on your mix of ACH and cards.
  5. Check export quality. You will leave someday. Hostages are not a feature.
  6. Decide what will still live outside the PMS: leasing, inspections, accounting, messaging.
  7. If those outside pieces are the real work, plan the orchestration layer before you go live, not after staff invent shadow trackers.

Keep human gates on refunds, deposit dispositions, and anything that changes owner money. Automate posting, reminders, and status writes once the rules are written.

How innflow fits an On-Site shop

innflow is the AI agent and workflow automation platform built for real work. Property teams use it to connect tools, run multi-step flows, and keep execution visible on a canvas. Agents use tools and carry context. They are not a second rent-roll.

On a small On-Site book, useful flows look like this:

  • When a charge posts and no payment arrives by the SLA, open a collection ticket and send the first notice.
  • When a work order sits with no vendor accept, escalate with the photos and unit history attached.
  • When a notice to vacate hits the inbox, start a move-out clock: inspection, deposit checklist, utility close, listing draft.
  • When a bill is uploaded, route approval by amount and property, then remind if it will miss the discount date.
  • Weekly, assemble an owner digest from charges, payments, and open work, for a human to send.

Keep On-Site as the system of record if you stay. If you migrate to a larger PMS later, keep innflow’s workflow definitions so you are not rebuilding tribal process inside the new vendor. Start with one path. Late rent after a posted charge is a good first flow because the trigger is clean and the metric is obvious.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is On-Site the same as RealPage OneSite?

No. OneSite is an enterprise multifamily platform. On-Site Property Manager is a lightweight, unit-tiered web PMS for smaller books. Mixing them up will waste a demo cycle.

How much does On-Site cost?

Software is sold in unit bands with a low published starting price for the smallest portfolios and the same core features across those early tiers. Confirm current bands and all payment fees before you budget. Directory screenshots go stale.

Can On-Site run commercial and residential together?

The vendor positions it for both. Commercial leases with CAM, percentage rent, or complex options will likely outgrow it. Simple commercial suites can fit.

When do we outgrow it?

When exceptions no longer fit the screens: multi-entity accounting, heavy leasing, a maintenance shop, or owners who need institutional packets. Volume alone is not the test. Complexity is.

Should we replace On-Site with innflow?

No. innflow orchestrates work across the tools you already use. Keep a system of record. Add agents for intake, SLAs, and handoffs the PMS will never own.

Conclusion

On-Site Property Manager is a coherent product for a small book: post charges, take online pay, track expenses, move people in and out, and send a work order from a browser. Review it on that job. Do not review it as an enterprise suite it never claimed to be. If the records are enough and the work is still messy, fix the workflow. If the records are not enough, move to a mid-market PMS on purpose.

When you want the work around those records to run with visible owners and agents you can inspect, deploy with innflow. Get Started at app.innflow.ai, or Talk to Sales at innflow.ai.

The Deposit Fight Is a File Problem

Move-out week is when "normal wear and tear" stops being a phrase and becomes a number on a ledger. Paint is faded. Carpet is tired. A door stick. A tile is loose. The resident wants the full deposit back. The owner wants the unit made rent-ready without eating every invoice. Maintenance wants a punch list, not a philosophy debate.

Most disputes are not won by arguing harder. They are won or lost on whether you can show the unit's condition at move-in, the condition at move-out, the age of the item, and a written rule that separates aging from negligence. If that packet is incomplete, you either under-charge (owners notice) or over-charge (residents sue, reviews drop, and you spend more in cycle time than the deduction was worth).

This guide is for operators, landlords, and portfolio teams who run turnovers at volume. It is operational guidance, not legal advice. Deposit rules, itemization deadlines, and what you may deduct vary by state and city. Counsel and your local statute control the money. Your job is to make the distinction between normal wear and tear and excessive tenant damages so consistent that two different community managers would reach the same charge on the same photos.

You will leave with HUD-style examples, useful-life logic for carpets and appliances, lease language that actually helps, and a move-out workflow innflow can orchestrate without hiding the human gate on money.

What Normal Wear and Tear Actually Means

Normal wear and tear is the deterioration that happens when a household uses a unit the way a unit is meant to be used. People walk on floors. They hang a few pictures. Paint oxidizes. Grout loosens. Cabinet doors swell. Plumbing clogs from age, not from a toy in the trap. HUD's working definition is useful: unavoidable aging from ordinary use, even when the resident is reasonably careful.

Excessive tenant damage is different. It is loss caused by negligence, abuse, accident, unauthorized alteration, or failure to report a problem that then got worse. A faded carpet after five years is aging. A burn, a pet stain through the pad, or a tear from dragged furniture is damage. The same surface can hold both. That is why a photo without a date and a useful-life note is not enough.

The legal test in most states is not "does this look perfect." It is "did the resident return the premises in the condition they received, less ordinary wear." You cannot charge a resident to make a five-year unit look like a day-one model home. You also do not have to absorb holes, missing fixtures, or crayon murals as "character."

Why the line stays fuzzy

People disagree because the words are subjective and the unit is not a lab. One manager sees nail holes as ordinary. Another sees ten holes in one wall as abuse. One owner wants new paint after every twelve-month lease. The statute does not care about that preference. Time in unit matters. A six-month stay that leaves filthy walls is not the same as a four-year stay that leaves tired paint.

Write the standard down. Train to the photos, not to mood. If your team cannot explain a deduction in one sentence with an exhibit, do not take the money.

Side-by-Side Examples Operators Can Train On

Use these as a field guide, not as a statute. Local law and the lease still win. Train inspectors to name the item, the cause, and the evidence.

Normal wear and tear

  • Faded, peeling, or cracked paint, including ceiling paint that aged in place
  • Small nail or pin holes from ordinary hanging
  • Hairline wall cracks from settling
  • Sticky cabinet doors, worn drawer slides, loose grout or tiles from age
  • Hardwood that needs a coat of finish, not a patch for gouges
  • Thin or faded carpet with no burns, tears, or pet saturation
  • Rusty shower rod, lightly worn enamel, faded shades
  • Clogged sink from old plumbing, not from foreign objects
  • Window issues caused by a failed frame or foundation movement

Excessive tenant damages

  • Unauthorized paint colors, murals, crayon, or wallpaper the owner did not approve
  • Large holes in drywall, plaster, or ceiling
  • Gouged hardwood, missing or cracked bathroom tile from impact
  • Broken windows, doors off hinges, missing fixtures or hardware
  • Carpet burns, stains, holes, or pet damage through the pad
  • Toilet clogged or cracked from improper objects
  • Chipped or broken sink and tub enamel
  • Torn, stained, or missing lamps and shades; bent or missing shower rods
  • Missing appliances, screens, or smoke detectors that were present at move-in

Pets do not automatically equal damage. Authorized pets still create ordinary wear. Unauthorized pets, urine, chewed trim, and flea treatment are usually damage. Document the lease permission separately from the condition photos.

Useful Life: You Rarely Charge Full Replacement

Even when the resident caused the loss, you generally charge remaining useful life, not a brand-new item. A nine-year refrigerator that dies after resident abuse is not a new refrigerator invoice. HUD-style useful life is a common training baseline. Confirm your company's schedule with counsel and your insurer.

  • Water heaters and air conditioners: about 10 years
  • Refrigerators: about 10 years
  • Ranges: about 20 years
  • Plush carpet: often 5 years in family housing, longer in senior housing
  • Interior enamel paint: often 5 years in family housing
  • Interior flat paint: often 3 years in family housing
  • Tile or linoleum: often 5 years in family housing
  • Shades, screens, and blinds: often about 3 years

If the item is past useful life, the deduction should be small or zero unless the resident created a disposal or emergency cost you would not otherwise have had. If the item was new at move-in, keep the invoice in the unit file. Age without a receipt is how residents win the argument.

Cleaning, carpet, paint, and bulbs

Routine turnover cleaning is usually the owner's cost. You may pass through extra labor when the unit was left unsanitary beyond ordinary use: grease baked into appliances, trash left behind, biohazard, or a cleaner who had to do a second pass because the resident never cleaned at all. Put the "broom-clean plus" standard in the lease so you are not inventing it at move-out.

Carpet cleaning is the grayest line in the building. Ordinary soil after a normal lease is wear. Saturated pet urine, burns, and irremovable stains are damage. You usually cannot charge a full replacement on a carpet that was already halfway through its life. Charge remaining life, keep the quote, and photograph the stain with a scale (a tape measure in the frame beats a close-up that looks like abstract art).

Paint follows time. After several years, a repaint is maintenance. After a short stay with dirt films, drawings, or unauthorized color, a repaint can be a charge. Light bulbs that worked at move-in and are dead at move-out are a resident item in most houses. Treat them as a checklist, not a surprise invoice.

Security Deposits Only Work If the File Works

The deposit is not a penalty. It is a limited fund for unpaid rent, cleaning beyond ordinary use, and damage beyond wear. Typical practice is about one month's rent, subject to local caps. If there is no qualifying deduction, the money goes back on the statutory clock. Late itemizations and sloppy math create statutory damages in some states. Speed is part of compliance.

A defendable deduction packet usually contains:

  • Signed move-in inspection with photos or video
  • Signed move-out inspection with matching angles
  • Lease clauses that define cleaning, alterations, and deposit use
  • Vendor invoices or unit-price schedule, not round numbers from memory
  • Useful-life calculation for replaced items
  • Itemized statement that maps each dollar to a photo and a cause

Do not mix owner upgrades into the resident bill. If you are replacing builder-grade vinyl with luxury vinyl because you wanted to, that is capex. If you are patching a hole the resident made, that is a charge. Mixing the two is how you lose the whole statement.

Lease Language That Makes the Call Easier

A vague "no damage" clause does not help a court or a resident. Put the operating rules in the lease and walk them at move-in. At minimum cover:

  • How move-in and move-out inspections are scheduled, signed, and photographed
  • What "ordinary cleanliness" means on the last day
  • Whether carpet cleaning is required, and when a professional invoice is chargeable
  • Alterations, paint, and hardware the resident may not change
  • How post-vacate damage discovered after keys are returned will be noticed
  • How the deposit is held, itemized, and returned
  • Pet, smoking, and unauthorized occupant rules that create specific damage types

Hand the resident a one-page wear-versus-damage sheet at walkthrough. Use the same sheet your inspectors use. Consistency is the product. A binder of custom exceptions is how two buildings in the same portfolio charge differently for the same nail hole.

How to Run Wear-and-Tear Decisions Operationally

Name a process owner for deposit chargebacks. Shared ownership is how itemization deadlines die while leasing thinks maintenance "has the photos." The owner does not photograph every unit. They own the standard, the SLA, and the exception queue.

Intake that a stranger can audit

Every move-out file needs structured fields: property and unit, lease start and end, occupancy length, pet status, move-in inspection ID, move-out inspection ID, claimed items, dollar amount, useful-life notes, and a terminal state (full refund, partial deduction, or dispute). Free-text notes can exist. They should not be the only record.

Photo discipline

Same rooms, same angles, lights on, wide shot then detail. Date stamps. Video for long corridors and flooring. Both parties should be invited to document. A resident video taken on move-out day is not an attack. It is a second camera you should welcome. After keys, the site team shoots again before vendors start so you can separate resident condition from vendor condition.

Human gates

Automate reminders and packet assembly. Do not automate the deduction decision. A person reviews anything over your internal threshold, any habitability-adjacent claim, any fair-housing-sensitive situation, and any file missing move-in photos. Package the brief: photos, invoices, useful-life math, and the deadline. Do not send "can you look at 12B."

Scoreboard that changes behavior

Track time from keys-in to itemized statement, percent of files with complete photo pairs, dispute rate, and rework (deductions reversed after a challenge). Ticket count is vanity. Late statements and reversed charges are the operating truth. Review the five most expensive disputes each month and change the standard if two inspectors would have called it differently.

Screening still matters, but it is not a personality contest and it is not a wear-and-tear shortcut. Credit, rental history, and income are the legal tools. Appearance and "vibes" are how teams wander into fair housing trouble. Wear-and-tear risk is managed with inspections and clauses, not with illegal proxies.

How innflow Fits the Chargeback Workflow

innflow is the AI agent and workflow platform built for real work. Agents connect to your system of record, inspection tools, and vendor inbox, then run the move-out spine on a visible canvas. They are not a chatbot with a property theme. They carry context, call tools, and stop at human gates when money moves.

For wear-versus-damage work, typical innflow patterns include:

  • Intake a notice-to-vacate and open a structured move-out file with required photo fields
  • Remind the site team to complete move-out media within the SLA, then flag missing angles
  • Assemble a chargeback brief: move-in set, move-out set, invoices, and useful-life notes
  • Route deductions above a dollar threshold to a regional manager with the full packet
  • Draft the itemized resident statement for human approval, then log the send date
  • Escalate files approaching the statutory return deadline before the clock dies

Keep the PMS as the ledger. innflow orchestrates the handoffs so the deposit decision is inspectable. Start with one path: notice to vacate through itemized statement. One owner. One cycle-time metric. Then expand to vendor dispatch and owner recap letters.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I deduct normal wear and tear from a security deposit?

Generally no. Ordinary aging (faded paint, worn carpet, small nail holes) is the owner's maintenance cost. Deposits are for unpaid amounts and damage beyond ordinary use. Confirm the statute and itemization rules in your state before you withhold.

Who decides if something is wear or damage?

Your written standard should decide first, using move-in and move-out evidence and useful life. If the resident disputes and you cannot settle, a court or agency may decide. That is why photos, invoices, and a consistent training sheet matter more than a manager's memory.

Can I charge for a full carpet or appliance replacement?

Usually only the remaining useful life, unless the item was new and totally destroyed. Keep purchase dates and invoices in the unit file. Charging a new carpet against a six-year install is how deductions get reversed.

What if we have no move-in photos?

Treat that as an exception, not a hunting license. Without a baseline, many deductions will not hold. Refund more, charge less, and fix intake so the next file has a signed inspection before keys are issued.

How should teams use AI on deposit files?

Use agents for intake, reminders, packet assembly, and deadline watches. Keep a human on the deduction, the resident letter, and any fair-housing-sensitive file. Visible workflows beat an opaque recommendation no one can defend.

Conclusion

Normal wear and tear versus excessive tenant damages is not a vibe. It is a documented comparison of two points in time, adjusted for the age of the item and the words in the lease. Train to examples. Charge remaining life. Return what you cannot prove. Run the file on a clock.

When you are ready to operationalize move-out intake, photo completeness, and itemization SLAs, deploy with innflow: connect your tools, automate the spine, and keep the money decision visible. Get Started at innflow.ai or app.innflow.ai, or Talk to Sales for a guided rollout across communities.

May 2022 Was When Recurring Work Stopped Being a Spreadsheet

The May 2022 wave of property management software features was not flashy. It was the month a lot of platforms finally treated operators like they run calendars, not one-off tickets. Recurring work orders. Recurring bills. Management fee invoices that match the contract. Owner statements you can send without rebuilding Excel. Optional two-factor authentication so the bookkeeper and the leasing lead are not forced into the same security posture.

Four years later, those capabilities are table stakes in a serious PMS. Teams still fail them. Filters get changed and nobody notices. Recurring PMs exist in the system and still happen on a paper clipboard. Owner packets go out late because someone is merging PDFs after hours. The feature shipped. The operating system around the feature did not.

This is not a vendor recap and it is not a rip-and-replace pitch. Property management software remains the system of record for leases, ledgers, and work orders. innflow sits beside that record: agents and workflows that take a feature from "available in the menu" to "actually runs every Tuesday." If you are evaluating software in 2026, read May 2022 as a checklist of workflows you still have to own.

You will leave with what each 2022 feature class was for, how operators still break it, and how to run recurring maintenance, payables, fees, and owner reporting without hiding exceptions.

What That 2022 Feature Set Was Trying to Fix

Before recurring objects were first-class, coordinators cloned last month's work order, hoped the vendor still existed, and posted bills when someone remembered. Management fees were a spreadsheet formula that drifted from the management agreement. Owners got a packet when the accountant had a quiet Friday. Security was all-or-nothing: 2FA for everyone or for no one.

May 2022-style releases attacked that mess in five places:

  • Recurring tasks and work orders: daily, weekly, or monthly PM that should not be retyped
  • Recurring bills and expenses: the same vendor obligation, posted on a clock
  • Management fees: flat, percent, or blended, then an owner invoice from the rule
  • Owner statements: cash flow, P&L, and transaction detail in PDF or Excel
  • Optional two-factor authentication: security per user, not a blunt company switch

Smaller companion features showed up in the same season: custom application terms, faster lease-payment entry, per-applicant settings, eviction tracking, bill-pay overrides when an account is short, choosing which bank pays a bill, a recurring-transaction detail report, applicant resubmits without a second fee, and search by reference number. None of that is strategy. All of it is cycle time if you actually use it.

In 2026 the interesting question is not "does our PMS have recurring work orders." It is "who owns the recurrence, what happens when it fails, and which agent packages the exception."

Recurring Work Orders: Preventive Maintenance as a Calendar

Recurring work orders exist so filter changes, detector checks, landscaping, trash, and unit turns that follow a pattern are not tribal knowledge. You set the interval, the property, the trade, and the expected completion window. The system should spawn the next ticket before the last one ages out.

Operators still break this in three ways. They create recurrences and never assign a vendor. They let a seasonal job keep firing in the off-season. They treat a no-show as a closed ticket because the due date passed. A recurrence without a confirmation state is a reminder, not a workflow.

Design the object with four stages:

  • Intake: property, asset or unit, trade, interval, season window, vendor, SLA
  • Decision: skip this cycle, split a batch, or escalate a failed visit
  • Execution: dispatch, access notes, parts, resident notice if entry is required
  • Confirmation: photo or checklist, close, spawn or hold the next occurrence

Name an owner for the preventive calendar (usually a maintenance lead, not "the board"). Review skipped cycles weekly. If HVAC filters are "recurring" and the building still has dirty racks, the software is not the constraint.

Recurring Bills: Payables That Match Reality

Recurring bills are the accounting twin of recurring work. Landscaping, pest, trash, elevator, alarm, software, and insurance installments should post without a coordinator re-keying the same invoice. The feature only works if the vendor, GL, property allocation, and bank account are correct on the template.

Watch the failure modes. A rate change that nobody updates. A contract that ended while the recurrence kept posting. A bill that posts to the wrong property after a sale. An override that pays from the operating account because trust funds were short, then nobody books the correction. The 2022-era "override insufficient funds" and "choose the paying bank" controls exist because those mistakes already happened.

Minimum controls:

  • One template owner per vendor family
  • A change log when amount, GL, or property split moves
  • A monthly exception list: recurrences that posted with no matching work, or work with no bill
  • A human gate on any override that spends from a different bank than the template

A recurring-transaction detail report (future charges by account) is how a controller sees next month before cash gets tight. If nobody opens that report, you do not have a forecast. You have a feature.

Management Fees: The Contract Has to Equal the Invoice

Fee engines that support flat, percent of collections, or a blend were a direct answer to "we invoice owners from a spreadsheet and hope it matches the agreement." The software should create the owner invoice from the rule and leave an audit trail.

Percent of what? Collected rent, billed rent, or rent plus other income? Does the fee apply to vacancies? Is there a minimum? A setup fee? A lease-up premium? If those answers live in a PDF that accounting has not opened this year, the feature will produce a number that is wrong in a confident font.

Operational rules:

  • Code the management agreement into the fee object when the owner is onboarded, not at month-end
  • Version the rule when the agreement amends. Do not silently edit last month's template
  • Reconcile fee invoices to the agreement quarterly, not only when an owner complains
  • Keep a human gate on waived fees, one-off credits, and any fee that hits a new owner in month one

innflow should not invent a second fee ledger. It should notice when the PMS posted a fee that does not match the stored agreement fields and package that exception for the portfolio accountant.

Owner Statements: Transparency Is a Delivery Workflow

Owner statements package cash flow, profit and loss, and a transaction list. PDF for most owners. Excel for the ones who rebuild their own model. The 2022 promise was "send the packet without a fire drill." The 2026 reality is that owners still email "where's my statement" because the workflow dies after the report is generated.

A statement is not done when the report exists. It is done when the right owner entity received the right period, the bank rec is closed enough to stand behind the cash line, and exceptions (large capex, insurance proceeds, owner draws) have a one-line explanation. Sending a raw dump is how you generate a Tuesday of inbound questions.

Run statements as a close process:

  1. Lock the period or freeze the recurrences that still need review
  2. Confirm bank and deposit matching for the properties in the batch
  3. Generate cash flow, P&L, and register
  4. Attach a short exception note for outliers
  5. Deliver in the owner's chosen format
  6. Log send time and bounce-backs

Measure cycle time from period end to owner receipt, not "reports run." If one accountant is still exporting by hand for a VIP owner, that is an exception path. Name it. Do not pretend the feature covers it.

Optional 2FA and the Quiet Security Work

User-level two-factor authentication was the grown-up version of "we turned on 2FA and the field techs could not log in." Optional per user is not optional security. It is a policy: who must use it (anyone who can move money, export owner data, or change bank accounts) and who may be phased in (read-only leasing on a shared office device, with a plan to retire that device).

Pair 2FA with the other 2022 hygiene items: reference-number search so you can find a disputed payment, eviction tracking so legal status is not a sticky note, and application settings that do not force every prospect through the same addenda. Those are access and compliance features. Treat them like you treat keys.

How to Run a Feature Rollout Without Burning the Team

Buying or turning on a module is not adoption. Pick one high-volume recurrence (filters, or landscaping bills, or monthly owner packets). Document the current path. Baseline cycle time for two to four weeks. Then turn the software object on and put an agent on the reminders and the exception package.

Owners of the work:

  • Maintenance lead: recurring work orders and skipped-cycle review
  • AP or accounting: recurring bills, bank selection, overrides
  • Controller or portfolio accountant: management fees and owner statements
  • IT or office manager: 2FA policy and user exceptions

Human gates stay on fee waivers, bank overrides, owner letters that explain a bad month, and any eviction-status change. Agents can draft and route. They should not silently post money or change legal status.

Common pitfalls: automating a notification that the work is late without fixing dispatch; measuring tickets created instead of jobs confirmed; training only the person who configured the recurrence; leaving 2FA off for the user who can cut owner checks.

How innflow Fits on Top of the PMS

innflow is the AI agent and workflow platform built for real work. Keep your property management software as the system of record. Use innflow to connect that record to email, vendor tools, and owner delivery, then run multi-step flows on a canvas you can inspect. Agents are not a chatbot bolted onto a report. They use tools, carry context, and stop where you place a gate.

For this feature set, typical innflow patterns include:

  • Watch recurring work orders that miss confirmation and package a vendor no-show brief
  • Match recurring bills to contracts and flag amount or property-split drift
  • Compare posted management fees to stored agreement fields before statements go out
  • Assemble owner statement packets, attach exception notes, and log delivery
  • Remind users who can move money to complete 2FA enrollment
  • Open an eviction-tracking file when a legal status field changes, with the ledger attached

Start narrow. One recurrence family. One metric (cycle time to confirmed PM, or hours from period close to owner send). One owner. Prove the spine, then scale complex workflows with innflow across the portfolio.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do we still need a PMS if we have workflow automation?

Yes. Property management software holds leases, trust accounting, and work-order history. innflow orchestrates the work around those records. Replacing the ledger to get better reminders is the expensive way to solve a handoff problem.

Which May 2022 feature should a growing team turn on first?

Pick the recurrence that already exists as tribal knowledge. For most multifamily shops that is preventive work orders or monthly owner statements. Recurring bills follow once the vendor list is clean. Fees follow once agreements are coded. 2FA should not wait if users can move money.

How do we keep recurring tickets from becoming noise?

Require a confirmation state, a skip reason, and a weekly review of skipped or failed cycles. If nobody looks at exceptions, turn the volume down until the owner of the calendar is real.

Is optional 2FA enough in 2026?

Optional is a rollout tool, not a security strategy. Mandate it for anyone with banking, owner PII, or admin rights. Phase the rest. Review exceptions the same way you review key control.

How is innflow different from a report scheduler?

A scheduler emits a file. innflow runs the steps around the file: completeness checks, exception notes, approvals, delivery, and escalation when a send fails. The canvas shows who owns the stalled packet.

Conclusion

The new property management software features of May 2022 were a bet that operators would rather run calendars than clone tickets. Recurring work, recurring payables, fee rules, owner packets, and user-level security still define whether a PMS is doing real work or storing it. Features do not close the period. Owned workflows do.

When you are ready to put agents on the spine (recurrence exceptions, fee checks, statement delivery), deploy with innflow. Get Started at innflow.ai or app.innflow.ai, or Talk to Sales if you want a guided rollout across markets.

Pests Are a Habitability Ticket, Not a Janitorial Nuisance

A roach report is not a "please buy traps" chat. It is a habitability, health, and asset-protection event. Bed bugs jump units. Mice follow pipe chases. Termites eat structure. One ignored kitchen becomes a stack complaint, a health-department notice, and a week of access fights while you try to treat three floors at once.

Operators lose these files when they argue philosophy ("the tenant brought them") instead of running a process: intake, inspection, licensed treatment, prep cooperation, follow-up, and a written decision on who pays. Lease language matters. Local code often matters more. In many jurisdictions you cannot waive the duty to keep the unit livable, even if the lease says "tenant handles all pests."

This guide is for landlords, community managers, and portfolio teams. It is practical process, not legal advice. State statutes, city health codes, and your counsel control who must pay and how fast you must act. Your job is to make tenant and landlord pest control responsibilities so explicit that a night tech and a regional manager would open the same work order.

innflow will not spray a unit. It will keep the report from dying in a group text: structured intake, vendor SLA, access notices, and a visible handoff when treatment fails.

What Pest Control Means in a Rental in 2026

Pest control is the work of preventing, identifying, and eliminating organisms that harm health, belongings, or the building. In multifamily, the common list is cockroaches, bed bugs, rodents, ants, fleas, and termites. Methods range from sanitation and exclusion (sealing gaps) to baits, traps, and licensed chemical treatment. Climate, trash practice, moisture, and the building envelope decide how often you will see the same pest twice.

The implied warranty of habitability is the legal spine in most states: the owner must deliver and maintain a unit that is fit to live in. Serious infestations (especially roaches, rodents, and bed bugs) usually sit inside that duty. Local codes may set response windows, require licensed operators, or name bed bugs as a specific violation class. Some cities require written bed-bug disclosures and a duty to eradicate and prevent reinfestation.

Tenants are not spectators. They must keep the unit reasonably clean, store food, take out trash, report early, and prepare for treatment. They are not the exterminator of last resort because a lease paragraph said so. Courts have rejected attempts to push the entire habitability duty onto the resident.

Who usually pays

Default rule of thumb, subject to local law: the landlord pays to inspect and treat unless you can prove the resident caused the condition through sanitation failure, hoarding, or bringing infested belongings, and the statute lets you charge. Proof is hard. Bed bugs in a mid-rise rarely have a single author. Moisture from a leaking stack is an owner problem even if the kitchen is messy. Treat first. Argue cost second, with photos and a vendor report, not with a vibe.

Landlord Responsibilities

Deliver the unit pest-free at move-in. That means a vacant treatment when the last file was dirty, a documented inspection, and no "we will handle it after you unpack." Recurring preventive service in common areas is cheaper than a building-wide bed-bug event.

Maintain the envelope and the moisture: seal pipe penetrations, door sweeps, weeps, and utility chases; fix leaks and damp storage; keep trash rooms closed and on a real pickup cadence. A bait station in a wet trash room is theater.

When a resident reports, investigate on a clock. Visit, look at adjacent units, and bring a licensed vendor when the pest is medical or structural (bed bugs, roaches in volume, rodents, termites). Hire licensed and insured operators. Require a written scope: target pest, units included, prep sheet, re-entry time, and follow-up date.

Follow up. One spray is not a close. Recurrence is common. Schedule the revisit, ask the resident whether activity continues, and treat neighbors when the biology says you must. Document every access attempt. A "we tried, they were not home" note without dates is how you lose a habitability claim.

If the same unit keeps failing, change the method. Different product, heat, or a prep-enforcement path. Do not close the ticket because you are tired of it.

Tenant Responsibilities

Sanitation is the resident's daily job: dishes, sealed food, liners in cans, no bags on the balcony, litter boxes, and no grease films that feed roaches. Clean cabinets and under the fridge. This is not optional politeness. It is how you avoid being the cause in a chargeback conversation.

Report early and in writing. Photos of droppings, bites, live insects, or gnaw marks. Dates. Unit number. A phone call that nobody logged is not notice. Good intake protects the resident as much as the owner: once notice is in the system, the SLA starts.

Cooperate with treatment. Prep sheets exist because foam and dust cannot reach a room full of bags. Clear the kitchen line, launder bedding for bed bugs, crate pets, and give access for the follow-up. Refusal to prep is a lease-enforcement issue. It is not a reason for the owner to abandon habitability. Document the refusal, reset the appointment, and escalate through the same notice path you use for other access problems.

Follow post-treatment instructions: leave baits in place, do not wipe residuals the vendor told you to leave, bag and heat-treat or dispose as instructed, and report new activity instead of buying a fogger that drives pests into the next stack.

Pest by Pest: How Operators Should Route the Work

Cockroaches

Roaches are a sanitation-plus-structure pest. They ride in groceries and they live in voids. Habitability usually puts treatment on the owner, especially if more than one unit is involved. Pair gel bait and growth regulators with exclusion and a trash-room fix. Charge the resident only with a clean file: vendor notes on food, grease, and refusal to prep, plus photos, and only if the lease and local law allow.

Bed bugs

Treat bed bugs as a building event until proven otherwise. Many states and cities put eradication on the owner. Some (including several disclosure statutes) make it difficult or illegal to bill the resident without proof they imported them. Inspect adjacent units. Use a licensed operator. Issue a prep sheet. Heat or a proper chemical protocol beats a store spray. Do not delay while you debate "who brought them." Delay is how you buy a floor.

Rodents

Mice and rats are an envelope problem first. Seal, bait, and clean. High activity plus droppings in a kitchen is a health issue. Owner pays for exclusion and treatment. Resident pays only for sanitation failures that are documented and chargeable under the lease. Check the trash chute and the ground-floor utility rooms every time, not just the complaining unit.

Ants, fleas, and termites

Ants are often moisture and food. Fleas usually mean a pet. Termites are structure and almost never a resident bill. Route termites to a specialist and a capital conversation. Route fleas with the pet addendum and a unit-plus-common-area plan so you do not treat 3B while the hallway carpet remains a reservoir.

Lease Clauses That Help (and Ones That Do Not)

Write clauses that allocate duties you can actually perform:

  • Resident must report pests in writing within a stated window
  • Resident must complete a reasonable prep sheet and provide access
  • Owner will use licensed vendors and may enter on proper notice
  • Preventive service schedule for common areas, if you provide one
  • When, if ever, a documented resident-caused infestation can be charged
  • No self-applied foggers without written approval

Do not write "tenant is solely responsible for all pests at all times" and expect it to survive a bed-bug or rodent case. Habitability and health codes often override that sentence. A clause that tries to waive livability is how you look reckless in front of a housing inspector.

How to Run Pest Control as an Operation

Name one process owner (usually the maintenance or community manager, with a regional backup for building-wide events). Shared ownership is how a Friday roach ticket sits until Monday while the stack next door lights up.

Intake fields

Require pest type (or "unknown"), unit, how long seen, photos, adjacent-unit risk, medical notes the resident chooses to share, pets, and access windows. Severity should be structured: bed bugs and rodents outrank a single ant trail.

SLA and exceptions

Set response targets by pest. Bed bugs and rodents get same-day or next-business-day vendor contact. Seasonal ants can wait in a defined queue. Exceptions that need a human: refusal of access, a resident who wants to hire their own unlicensed sprayer, a chargeback, a health-department letter, and any infestation that crosses three or more units.

Scoreboard

Time to first vendor appointment, time to confirmed clear, revisit rate, units treated per event, and open tickets older than your SLA. Do not celebrate ticket volume. Celebrate closed biology and fewer repeats in the same stack.

This is not legal advice. If a resident withholds rent, calls the health department, or claims bites and medical harm, loop counsel and keep the file complete: notices, photos, vendor reports, and access logs.

How innflow Fits Pest Workflows

innflow is the AI agent and workflow platform built for real work. Agents connect your maintenance inbox, PMS, vendor portal, and notice templates, then run multi-step pest flows on a canvas. They are not a chatbot that tells someone to buy traps. They classify the report, open the work order, attach the prep sheet, and escalate a missed access window with the full history.

Typical innflow patterns for pest control:

  • Triage inbound messages into pest type and severity before a human touches the queue
  • Open adjacent-unit inspection tasks when the pest is bed bugs or rodents
  • Send prep instructions and entry notices, then watch for unconfirmed appointments
  • Package a chargeback brief only when vendor notes and photos support a resident-caused claim
  • Digest weekly: open infestations, SLA breaches, and stacks with repeat activity

Keep the PMS as the work-order record. innflow orchestrates the spine so a habitability file is inspectable. Start with one pest path (bed-bug intake through follow-up). One owner. One cycle-time metric. Then expand.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is pest control the landlord's or the tenant's job?

Both, in different layers. The owner generally must deliver a livable, pest-controlled building and treat serious infestations. The resident must clean, report, and prepare. Local code can override a lease that dumps all cost on the tenant. Confirm with counsel in your market.

Who pays for bed bug treatment?

Often the landlord, unless a statute and a strong file show the resident imported them and allow a charge. Treat immediately either way. Delay while you assign blame is how one unit becomes a floor.

Can a lease make the tenant responsible for all pests?

You can allocate some duties and some costs. You usually cannot waive habitability. Clauses that say the resident handles every infestation, including structure and neighboring units, are a dispute magnet. Write reporting, prep, and documented chargeback rules instead.

What should residents do before the vendor arrives?

Follow the written prep sheet: clear treatment surfaces, launder bedding for bed bugs, secure food and pets, and stay out for the re-entry window. Photograph compliance if you expect a dispute. Report if you cannot prep so the appointment can be reset, not wasted.

How can AI agents help without hiding the file?

Use agents for classification, notices, SLA watches, and exception packets. Keep a human on chargebacks, health-department responses, and any decision to enter after refused access. Visible workflows are the point.

Conclusion

Navigating pest control is a split of duties, not a blame contest. Landlords own habitability, exclusion, licensed treatment, and follow-up. Tenants own sanitation, prompt notice, and prep. The building wins when those jobs are written, timed, and documented.
