People still search Cozy vs. Avail. Cozy, as a product, is already gone

Type Cozy vs Avail into a search bar and you will get a property management software comparison written for 2018. Independent landlords really did pick between those two brands for listings, applications, and ACH rent. That pairing is outdated in a specific way: Cozy the standalone company was acquired and folded into Apartments.com Rental Manager after CoStar bought it in 2021. Accounts migrated. The Cozy name faded. The workflow questions did not.

Avail is still a live product, now part of the Realtor.com network. Apartments.com Rental Manager is the successor most former Cozy users actually log into. A honest 2026 comparison is therefore Avail versus Apartments.com Rental Manager, with Cozy treated as the history that still drives the query. If you are a third-party manager running a full PMS, neither tool is your system of record. If you are a small landlord who wants listings, screening, a lease, and rent collection without hiring a firm, one of them might be.

This article compares the two on listings, applications, screening, leases, rent, maintenance, accounting, and price. It stays operational. Feature tables without a workflow still leave you with unanswered guest cards and unsigned addenda. innflow is not a Cozy replacement and not an Avail replacement. It is the AI agent and workflow layer you put on top of whatever system of record you keep, when the work spans tools and people.

What each product is, and who it is for

Apartments.com Rental Manager (the Cozy successor) is a listing-led landlord toolkit inside a large rental marketplace. Its gravity is traffic on the Apartments.com network. You can list, take an application, screen, e-sign a lease, and collect rent. The brand renters already know is the point. Customization is thinner. In-platform messaging and deeper accounting are not the reason you pick it.

Avail is an end-to-end DIY landlord platform: syndication across many listing sites, configurable applications, TransUnion screening, state-specific leases, rent collection with optional credit reporting, a maintenance thread, and a basic accounting dashboard. The free tier is the hook. Unlimited Plus, priced per unit on Avail's public page, buys faster deposits, waived ACH fees, more lease control, and priority support.

Neither product is a full property management system for a growing third-party shop. Trust accounting, owner statements, and multi-entity books are the usual breaking points. If you manage hundreds of units for dozens of owners, you are shopping in the wrong aisle. If you own a handful of doors and want rent out of a personal checking account, you are in the right aisle.

A note on names so the rest of this piece stays readable

When this article says "Cozy," it means the product people remember and the Apartments.com Rental Manager workflow that replaced it. When it says "Avail," it means Avail as it exists now under Realtor.com. Feature sets change. Verify price and syndication lists on the vendor sites before you buy. What follows is an operator comparison, not a partnership endorsement.

Feature-by-feature: Cozy (Apartments.com) vs Avail

Listings and demand

Cozy's successor lists primarily into the Apartments.com family (including sister sites in that network). Paid upgrades can add video or better placement. The bet is simple: renters already search that brand, so you live where they are.

Avail syndicates more widely, including Realtor.com and a long list of rental sites, with tour scheduling and optional promoted listings. The bet is coverage. More boards, more inbound, more need for a single place to work the lead so you do not answer the same question four times.

Operator implication: if your units already lease from one marketplace, Cozy's successor can be enough. If you bleed days vacant because the listing is only in one window, Avail's syndication is the more interesting half of the comparison. Neither tool fixes a unit that is not showable or photos that are two turns old.

Applications and screening

Apartments.com Rental Manager uses a standardized application. Custom questions are limited or absent. Screening is TransUnion-based. In the common setup, the applicant pays, and the landlord cannot always choose to absorb the fee. Reports are standardized (ResidentScore and related history), which is fine if your criteria fit the template.

Avail lets landlords pick which reports to run (credit, background, eviction) and, depending on plan, add custom questions. Automated prior-landlord reference requests exist. The landlord can choose who pays for screening. That flexibility is useful. It is also how a small shop accidentally screens two applicants two different ways.

If you care about fair housing, the winner is not "more custom questions." The winner is one written criteria sheet applied the same way every time. Avail gives you more knobs. You still need a process owner.

Leases

Both sides offer e-sign and state-aware templates. Avail leans harder on lawyer-reviewed, auto-updating state leases and the ability to upload your own document. Apartments.com offers local-compliant templates with lighter customization. If your counsel already has a lease, Avail's upload-and-sign path is closer to how professional shops work. If you have no counsel and no lease, either template is better than a blog post pasted into Word. Neither replaces a lawyer in a regulated city.

Rent collection

This is where small landlords actually feel the product every month.

On the Cozy successor, ACH is typically free to the landlord, card and wallet payments carry a tenant-paid percentage, and faster funding is an upgrade. One bank account per landlord profile is a common constraint. Rent reporting to credit bureaus has not been the headline feature.

On Avail, ACH often carries a small per-payment fee on the free tier, cards cost a higher percentage, AutoPay is built in, and CreditBoost can report on-time rent to TransUnion. Unlimited Plus is the path to next-day deposits, waived ACH fees, and multiple bank accounts.

Do the math on your book, not the landing page. A landlord with a few units and ACH-heavy residents may prefer Cozy's successor on raw payment cost. A landlord who wants faster funding and will pay per unit will look at Avail Plus. Neither tool is a lockbox or a genuine trust-accounting system.

Maintenance, messaging, and books

Avail keeps more of the operating week inside the product: in-app messages, a maintenance portal with photos and a history, and an accounting dashboard that logs rent and expenses and exports. Apartments.com Rental Manager is thinner here. Tenants can submit a request. Communication and repair tracking often leave the platform. Expense tracking exists but is basic.

If your pain is "I cannot find the thread where I told them the disposer would be Tuesday," Avail is the better of the two. If your pain is "I need owner packets, CAM, and three entities," neither product is the answer. You need a PMS, and then you still need a workflow layer.

Price, in plain language

Both lead with free for many residential landlords. Cozy's successor stays mostly free with limited upgrades. Avail stays free with a per-unit Unlimited Plus option, plus the payment fees above. Confirm current numbers before you commit. Price should not decide a 2-unit hobby and a 25-unit side business the same way.

Total cost is fees plus time. A free stack that dumps every lead into texts is not free. A paid tier that still rebuilds the application in email is not automation.

How to choose without a feature-score fantasy

Choose Apartments.com Rental Manager (the Cozy path) if:

  • Your residents already find you on that network.
  • You want free ACH more than you want in-app messaging.
  • A standard application and a standard lease are enough.
  • You will keep maintenance and books in other tools on purpose.

Choose Avail if:

  • You want broader syndication and tour scheduling in one login.
  • You need custom application questions or landlord-paid screening.
  • You want rent reporting, faster funding, or multiple bank accounts.
  • You want maintenance threads and a lightweight ledger in the same place.

Choose neither as your long-term system of record if you are a third-party manager, you have trust accounting, you run mixed commercial, or you need owner reporting that an accountant will sign. In that case, pick a real PMS and treat Cozy or Avail as, at most, a listing or payment sidecar you are prepared to replace.

The comparison most articles skip

Software buying is not the usual failure. Ownership, intake, and handoffs are. A landlord can pick Avail, still miss applications for 48 hours, and still send a lease that does not match the advertised special. A landlord can pick the Cozy successor, still track repairs in a group text, and still forget the adverse-action notice. The product does not install a process owner.

Write the unit of work before you switch tools: a completed application file, a signed lease, a posted payment, a closed work order. Name the SLA. Name the exception path. Then see which vendor's objects map to those units. If they do not, you will rebuild the process in email either way.

How to run DIY landlord software without burning the evenings

Even a 6-unit book needs a single process owner. If two partners both "handle leasing," SLAs die. Pick one person who owns the listing-to-lease path and one scoreboard:

  • Time to first response on a new inquiry
  • Time from complete application to decision
  • Days vacant after rent-ready
  • Work orders older than your own policy

Standardize intake. Every lead, every application, every repair gets the same fields: unit, type, severity, requested outcome. Free-text can exist. It cannot be the only record.

Design the exceptions: applicant wants to pay the fee later, screening comes back thin, a resident submits a repair that is really a habitability issue, a payment fails two days before late fees. For each, name the human decision and the clock. Then stop adding tools until those paths are written.

Common pitfalls in this exact comparison:

  • Migrating off Cozy's successor without exporting leases, payment history, and resident contacts first.
  • Running Avail screening without a written criteria sheet.
  • Advertising on five boards and answering from three inboxes.
  • Calling either product "accounting" when you mean a CSV for tax season.

How innflow fits if you keep Cozy's successor, Avail, or a PMS

innflow is the AI agent and workflow automation platform built for real work. Property teams use it to connect tools, run multi-step flows, and keep execution visible on a canvas. Agents are not chatbots with a landlord skin. They use tools, carry context, and complete tasks with structured logic you can inspect.

A Cozy vs Avail comparison is a systems-of-engagement comparison. innflow is orchestration on top:

  • Triage inbound leads from more than one listing site into one queue with a first-response SLA.
  • Check application completeness before you pay for or request screening.
  • Route maintenance photos to the right vendor and nudge stalls past your clock.
  • Draft resident updates from a payment or work-order event, with a human gate when tone matters.
  • Build a weekly exception digest (aging leads, unsigned leases, failed ACH, open turns) without copy-paste.

Keep Avail, Apartments.com, or a full PMS as the system of record. innflow does not pretend to replace listings or rent collection. It makes the work between those objects visible. Start with one path, usually lead-to-complete-application or vacant-to-rent-ready. Prove cycle time. Then expand.

Get Started at innflow.ai, or open the canvas at app.innflow.ai.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cozy still available as its own property management software?

No. Cozy was acquired and migrated into Apartments.com Rental Manager. People still use "Cozy vs Avail" as the search phrase. The live comparison is Avail versus that Rental Manager product. If you still have old Cozy logins or PDFs, export anything you need and treat the current Apartments.com account as the system you are actually comparing.

Which is cheaper, Cozy or Avail?

Both can be free at the entry tier. Your real cost is payment fees, optional paid listing or Plus features, and the hours you spend stitching inboxes. Avail's paid per-unit plan is the clearer upgrade ladder. Cozy's successor stays cheaper for some ACH-heavy landlords and thinner on operations features. Run last year's payment mix through both fee schedules.

Can either replace a professional property management system?

Not for third-party management, trust accounting, or multi-owner reporting. They are DIY landlord platforms with listing and payment strength. innflow is also not a PMS. It orchestrates work across the systems you already run.

Where should AI agents start if we use Avail or Apartments.com?

Start where the work is repetitive and data-rich: lead triage, application completeness, reminders on unsigned leases, and stalled work orders. Leave screening decisions, fair housing sensitive messages, and money exceptions to a person with a clean brief.

Should we switch tools just because Cozy changed brands?

Only if the successor is missing a job you actually do (syndication, messaging, faster deposits, custom applications). Switching tools without a written workflow recreates the same delays under a new logo. Map the path first, then change the vendor if the objects still do not fit.

Conclusion

Cozy vs Avail is a real property management software comparison with an expired brand on one side. Treat Cozy as Apartments.com Rental Manager. Compare listings, screening control, rent fees, and whether you need maintenance and books in the same login. Pick the tool that matches the unit of work you will actually run. If you have outgrown DIY platforms, step up to a PMS instead of stacking another landlord app.

When the bottleneck is handoffs rather than a missing listing board, deploy innflow on top of the system you keep: connect tools, automate multi-step flows, and keep execution visible. Get Started at innflow.ai, or Talk to Sales when you want a guided rollout across a portfolio.

The house you live in is not yet a rental asset

Listing your old home on a rental site is the easy part. The hard part is the conversion: lender permission, landlord insurance, city and HOA rules, a rent that actually covers the carrying cost, a lease that will stand up, and a tax file that starts the day the first tenant moves in. Miss any of those and you have a second job with legal exposure, not a passive investment.

This converting primary residence rental property complete guide is for owners who are relocating, trading up, or holding a home they do not want to sell yet. It walks the operating sequence, the tax treatment that changes on conversion day, and the first-year workflow that keeps the property from eating your nights. It is not legal, tax, or lending advice. Mortgage riders, municipal licenses, and IRS rules control. Sit with your lender, a local landlord attorney, and a CPA before you change occupancy.

Once the unit is live, the work is intake, screening, lease execution, rent collection, maintenance, and a clean books close. innflow belongs on that spine: agents and workflows that keep the conversion checklist and the first tenancy visible. It does not replace your lender, your PMS, or your accountant.

Why the conversion conversation is different in 2026

Owners convert a primary home when they cannot or will not sell: a job move, a family change, a market where listing would lock in a weak price, or a neighborhood with enough rent demand to cover the note. That math is tighter than it was a few years ago. Insurance is harder to place. Many cities added rental registration, inspection, or short-term-rental bans that also affect long-term use. HOAs have grown stricter about rental caps. Lenders still treat owner-occupied loans differently from investment loans.

The tax picture also changed the moment you stop living there. Schedule E reporting, depreciation, and the Section 121 home-sale exclusion all start a clock. If you later sell, the years as a rental can shrink the exclusion, and depreciation you took (or were allowed to take) is recaptured. The conversion is a finance decision and a compliance project, not a weekend listing task.

Confirm you are allowed to rent the house

Start with permission, not photos. Three files decide whether the conversion is legal: the loan, the insurance policy, and the local or association rules.

Mortgage and occupancy

Owner-occupied notes often require you to live in the home for a stated period, commonly around twelve months, and some riders restrict rental use. Call the servicer and ask, in writing, whether converting to a rental is allowed, whether occupancy affidavits still apply, and whether they will require a refinance to an investment-property loan. Investment pricing is usually higher. Do not assume silence is consent. A due-on-sale or occupancy clause is not something you want to discover after the tenant is in.

Insurance

A standard homeowners policy is written for you living there. Once a tenant occupies the home, you generally need landlord or dwelling-fire coverage plus liability that contemplates tenant-related claims. Tell the carrier the conversion date. Ask what happens to personal property you leave behind, whether loss of rents is available, and whether the policy requires a vacancy notice if the unit sits empty between occupants. Keep the binder and the declarations page in the property file.

City, county, state, and HOA rules

Many cities require a rental license, registration, or a habitability inspection before you collect rent. Some require smoke and carbon-monoxide certificates, lead disclosures, or a local landlord account. If the home sits in an HOA or condo regime, read the rental cap, minimum lease term, application package, and any ban on short-term stays. A community that allows only a fixed percentage of rentals can deny the lease even if the city would issue a license. Get written confirmation before you spend on paint and photos.

Build the deal around real numbers, not last year's mortgage payment

A converted residence looks cheap because you already own it. That hides the true cost. Price the unit as if you were buying it today as an investor.

  • Market rent. Pull comps for the same beds, baths, parking, and school zone. Your emotional attachment is not a rent survey.
  • Carrying cost. Principal and interest, taxes, insurance, HOA dues, utilities you will keep, lawn or snow, and a vacancy reserve.
  • Turn and capex. Paint, flooring, appliances, and the first deferred-maintenance list. A house you lived in for years has owner-grade wear that tenants will report on day one.
  • Management. Self-manage only if you can answer nights and weekends. A manager typically prices as a share of collected rent. Model both.
  • Reserves. A roof, HVAC, or sewer line does not wait for a good month. Hold cash outside the operating account.

If rent after vacancy and expenses does not cover the note plus reserves, you are subsidizing the house. That can still be a valid hold if you expect appreciation or you need time to sell into a better market. Call it a hold, not cash flow.

Prep the house as a rental, not as your home

Tenants will use the property harder than you did. Walk it as an inspector would, not as the person who already knows which window sticks.

  • Repair safety items first: smoke and CO detectors, GFCI where required, handrails, water-heater TPR, trip hazards, and lockable exterior doors.
  • Service HVAC, water heater, and any appliances that stay. Photograph serial numbers.
  • Neutralize the unit: holes patched, paint that photographs, flooring that will survive two leases.
  • Remove personal property you care about. What you leave becomes inventory you must track or a dispute at move-out.
  • Change locks or rekey after you move. Do not hand a tenant the key you used for a decade.
  • Document the empty unit with a dated room-by-room photo set. That file is the baseline for the security deposit.

If the city requires a pre-rental inspection, schedule it before listing. Failed inspections delay the lease and burn the applicant you just screened.

Lease, screening, and the first occupancy

Treat this like any other rental, even if the first tenant is a friend. Informal occupancy is how converted homes become expensive lawsuits.

Screen for credit, income, rental history, and identity using a consistent written criteria sheet. Fair housing applies the moment you advertise. Do not invent a different standard for someone who "seems fine" because they already know the neighborhood.

Use a lawyer-reviewed lease for your state: rent, due date, late fee, deposits, utilities, who maintains the yard, pet rules, occupancy limits, entry notice, and what happens at the end of the term. If the HOA has rules, attach them and require compliance. Collect the deposit and first month through a trackable method. Do not take cash you cannot prove.

On move-in day, complete a condition report with the tenant, not after they have lived there a week. Pair it with the photo set. That packet is what you will need if you later make a deposit claim.

Tax treatment starts on conversion day

Once the home is held out for rent, the IRS generally treats it as rental real estate. Report rent on Schedule E. Common deductions include mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, repairs, management fees, utilities you pay, advertising, and legal or accounting costs that belong to the rental. Keep a separate bank account from day one. Mixing personal and rental cash is how first-year books fail.

Depreciation

Residential rental buildings are generally depreciated over 27.5 years. Land is not depreciable. Your depreciable basis is typically the lower of fair market value at conversion or your adjusted basis, allocated between land and building. A simple illustration: a building portion of $275,000 depreciated straight-line over 27.5 years is about $10,000 a year. Your CPA should set the basis and the placed-in-service date. Do not guess from Zillow.

Section 121 and the sale you might still want

The primary-residence exclusion can still apply if you owned and used the home as your principal residence for at least two of the five years before sale, subject to other limits. After you move out, that five-year window keeps running. Many owners who want the exclusion sell within roughly three years of conversion so the two-of-five test still holds. Nonqualified-use rules and depreciation recapture can still tax part of the gain. Depreciation allowed or allowable after May 6, 1997 is generally not excludable and is often recaptured at a higher rate, commonly described as up to 25 percent. Model the sale with a CPA before you assume the exclusion will save the deal.

This is not tax advice. Filing status, partial-use years, 1031 exchanges, and state tax can change the answer. The point for operators is operational: start the depreciation file, keep invoices, and do not wait until April to reconstruct the conversion date.

How to run the conversion as an operation

Name one owner for the conversion project. If two spouses and a manager all "have it," the license expires and the insurance still says owner-occupied. The owner runs the checklist. Advisors (lender, broker, attorney, CPA) sit behind specific gates.

Intake and checklist

Treat the conversion as a ticket with required fields: target first-occupancy date, lender status, insurance status, license or HOA approval, basis memo from the CPA, rent comps, repair punch list, listing date, and screening criteria. Nothing moves to "listed" until the permission items are done.

Human gates

Automate reminders and document collection. Keep humans on: accepting a loan change, binding insurance, signing a lease, approving an applicant who fails a criterion, and any decision to sell instead of rent. Those are judgment and liability, not busywork.

Exceptions

Design them now: lender requires a refinance you cannot price, HOA rental cap is full, city inspection fails, the first applicant is a family member who wants a handshake lease, insurance will not bind until repairs are done, and a vacancy that lasts past the first mortgage due date. Each exception needs an owner, an SLA, and a packet (loan letter, HOA email, inspection report, cash-flow sheet).

Scoreboard

Days from decision to first rent received, open punch-list items, days vacant after ready, application-to-lease cycle time, and whether the books closed for the first rental month. Those measures tell you if the conversion is actually working. A photo of a listing is not a metric.

How innflow fits a residence-to-rental conversion

innflow is the AI agent and workflow automation platform built for real work. Agents connect to the tools you already use, run multi-step flows on a canvas, and keep execution visible. A conversion is a finite project that then becomes a recurring tenancy workflow. That is a poor fit for a chatbot and a good fit for orchestration.

Typical innflow patterns for this conversion: a checklist that will not mark the unit listable until lender, insurance, and license tasks are complete; collection of bids and photos against the punch list; a screening packet assembled for a human approval gate; lease and deposit reminders; a move-in inspection file that attaches the photo set; and a monthly digest of rent received, open work orders, and expenses that belong on Schedule E.

Keep the system of record for the lease and the ledger where it already lives. innflow orchestrates the handoffs around those systems. Start with the conversion checklist or the first move-in packet. Expand only after that path holds through one occupancy.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I have to live in the home for a year before I can rent it?

Many owner-occupied loans expect you to occupy for a stated period, often around twelve months, and some local programs have their own occupancy rules. That is a loan and program question, not a universal landlord statute. Read the note and ask the servicer in writing before you list.

Will converting to a rental change my mortgage rate?

It can. Some servicers allow the existing loan to remain. Others require an investment-property refinance with different pricing and reserves. Get the answer before you count on today's payment in the rent model.

Can I still use the $250,000 or $500,000 home-sale exclusion?

Possibly, if you still meet the two-of-five ownership and use tests and other Section 121 rules. Time as a rental can reduce the excluded gain, and depreciation is generally recaptured. Confirm with a CPA before you treat the exclusion as cash you already have.

Should I hire a property manager for a single converted home?

Hire one if you cannot meet the response SLA, you live in another city, or you will avoid hard conversations with tenants. Management fees are a real line item, often described in the market as a percentage of collected rent. Self-manage only if you will actually run screening, maintenance, and books on time.

Is this legal or tax advice?

No. Licensing, fair housing, lease law, lender rules, and federal and state tax treatment vary. Use licensed local counsel and a CPA who works with rental real estate before you convert occupancy or file the first return.

Conclusion

A converting primary residence rental property complete plan is permission, insurance, numbers, a tenant-ready unit, a real lease, and a tax file that starts on day one. The owners who regret the conversion skipped one of those and called the rest "passive income." The owners who keep the house treat it like an operating asset from the first listing photo.

When you are ready to run the conversion checklist and the first tenancy as a visible workflow, use innflow to connect tools, automate packets and reminders, and keep handoffs on the canvas. Get Started at innflow.ai or app.innflow.ai. Talk to Sales when you want the same conversion cadence across more than one home.

Condo Manager is an association back office, not a rental operating system

Boards and management companies shop HOA software when dues, owner ledgers, and meeting files live in three spreadsheets and a filing cabinet. Condo Manager sits in that category: accrual accounting, owner and unit records, meeting archives, and a building register aimed at self-managed associations and HOA-focused firms. It is not a multifamily leasing stack. If your pain is tenant screening, rent collection, and work-order SLAs across rental doors, you are evaluating the wrong product family.

This condo manager hoa management software reviews piece is for community managers, board treasurers, and operators who mix association work with a few rentals and need an honest map: what the product actually does, how pricing is sold, where reviews praise it, where they stall, and which alternatives fit which job. innflow is not a Condo Manager replacement and not a PMS. It is the orchestration layer you put on top of whichever system of record you keep.

Software comparisons fail when they score feature grids and ignore the work: assessment billing, delinquency, ARC requests, board packets, and vendor invoices. Judge Condo Manager against those jobs, then decide whether you still need a separate rental system and a workflow layer.

What Condo Manager is (and who it is for in 2026)

Condo Manager is property-management software designed around homeowner associations and self-managed communities. The design bet is user-friendliness for people who run corporations, units, and owner files, not leasing funnels. Management companies that live in assessments, reserves, and meeting minutes are the intended user. Rental-first operators are not.

That distinction matters more in 2026 than it did when desktop association packages were enough. Owners expect portals. Boards expect packets on time. Banks expect clean reconciliations. Mixed portfolios (HOA plus rentals) keep trying to force one product to do both association governance and landlord operations. Condo Manager leans association. Plan the stack accordingly.

Features that actually show up in the product

Accounting

The accounting suite is the core pitch: a true accrual system with receivables, payables, and a general ledger. Delinquent-account tracking is built for assessment collections, which is the cash engine of an HOA. Bank reconciliation is described as automatic across an unlimited number of accounts. Other finance tools include utility billing, budget management, profitability views, and digital check signatures.

For a treasurer, that is the right shape. For a landlord who needs security-deposit trust accounting and owner draws across rental units, confirm those workflows in a demo. Association ledgers and rental owner statements are not the same report with a different label.

Communication and statements

Mailing lists, letters, work-order notices, and a communication history sit in the same product. Automatic owner statements are the feature boards notice first, because "please send my ledger" is a weekly interruption. Record keeping is part of the communication design, which helps when a later dispute needs the paper trail.

Management records and meetings

Owner, corporation, and unit details are stored in separate areas rather than one noisy contact record. Meeting minutes can be archived. Repetitive office tasks are the automation target: the product is trying to be an office manager for mundane association work, not an AI leasing agent.

Building register and maintenance

The maintenance module tracks past work and can schedule preventative repairs. That is how you prove maintenance to an inspector, estimate real building cost, and keep insurance and code conversations grounded. It is a building register, not a resident-facing maintenance app with photos, vendor dispatch, and SLA clocks.

Condo Manager pricing

Pricing is quote-based. Public third-party writeups have put a starting point around $150 per month, which sits on the expensive side relative to small-association tools that publish $40 to $60 entry prices. Treat that figure as a research starting point, not a contract. Ask for implementation, training, payment-processing, and any per-community or per-door add-ons in the same quote.

A free trial exists, but it is not self-serve in the usual SaaS sense. You generally email the company to get access. A demo is the more common path. If you cannot get a written quote and a trial community that looks like yours, do not sign a multi-year deal on a slide deck.

Compare total cost of ownership, not the monthly teaser: conversion of historical ledgers, payment fees, extra modules, and the staff hours to learn a system that reviewers say is easy but still has reported glitches.

What reviews get right: pros and cons

Pros

  • Users call the platform user-friendly and say it organizes association data in a way that is easy to review.
  • The feature set fits homeowner associations, including communities that mix single-family lots with other property types.
  • The learning curve is described as manageable for office staff who are not professional accountants.

Cons

  • Customer support draws complaints about slow or unresponsive help, plus limited weekend and after-hours coverage. Association work does not stop on Friday at 5.
  • Reviewers report glitches. A ledger product that glitches during assessment runs is an operational risk, not a cosmetic issue.
  • Tenant-facing depth is thin. If you also operate rentals, expect to add another system for portals, applications, and resident maintenance.

Read those cons as design, not just quality. Condo Manager is built for owners and the association office. Tenants are not the primary user. Buying it to "also handle rentals" is how you end up with two half-used products.

How Condo Manager compares to real alternatives

Do not compare it only to other HOA brands or only to rental PMS tools. Split the job.

PayHOA and other small-association suites

Self-managed boards with a few dozen doors often want published pricing, online dues, and a simple owner portal. Tools in the PayHOA class typically start near $49 per month by unit tier. They will not match Condo Manager's accrual depth. They will be easier to buy and easier to abandon if the board turns over.

CINC, Vantaca, and Enumerate (TOPS)

Professional community-association firms usually short-list CAM platforms with portfolio accounting, lockbox and payments, violations, ARC, and board portals. CINC and Vantaca sell on custom quotes to management companies. Enumerate (formerly TOPS) is the long-running cloud suite in the same conversation. These are the peers if you are a management company, not a volunteer treasurer.

Innago

Innago is a free rental operations tool: online rent, e-sign leases, screening, and basic reporting. Feature depth is limited. It is a reasonable contrast if your real problem is landlord work, not HOA ledgers. It is not an association accounting replacement.

Hemlane

Hemlane prices from a base fee plus a per-unit charge (public tiers have been described around $28 plus $2 to $32 per unit, with monthly minimums). It is rental advertising, lease management, and rent collection. Again, different job than Condo Manager.

If your book is mostly associations, stay in the CAM family and judge Condo Manager against CINC, Vantaca, Enumerate, and lighter board tools. If your book is mostly rentals, do not buy Condo Manager to "grow into HOA later."

How to run an HOA software evaluation as an operation

Name one process owner for the selection: usually the portfolio controller or the head of community management. The board approves budget. The owner runs the scorecard.

Intake: define the unit of work

List the workflows that must survive go-live: assessment billing, ACH returns, delinquency notices, owner ledger requests, AP invoices, bank rec, work orders, ARC, violations, meeting packets, and year-end financials for the CPA. If a vendor cannot show those in a sandbox that looks like one of your communities, they are selling a tour, not a system.

Human gates

Data conversion, chart-of-accounts mapping, and the first live assessment run need a human gate. So does any decision to run rentals inside the same database. Do not let a salesperson "turn on tenants" as a checkbox.

Exceptions

Design them before you sign: failed bank file, owner who pays the wrong community, a mid-year manager takeover with dirty books, a support outage during coupon season, and a board that wants a custom report the product cannot produce. Each exception needs an owner, an SLA, and a fallback (manual ACH file, printed ledger, CPA workbook).

Scoreboard

Time to close the month, delinquency aging, owner statement cycle time, open work-order age, support ticket age, and whether the bank rec is done without a side spreadsheet. Those measures decide if Condo Manager is working. A feature checklist from the RFP does not.

How innflow fits next to Condo Manager

innflow is the AI agent and workflow automation platform built for real work. Agents connect to tools, run multi-step flows on a canvas, and keep execution visible. That is the layer association teams still lack after they buy a ledger: packets, exceptions, and handoffs across email, the CAM system, the bank, and the board.

Typical innflow patterns around an HOA system of record: intake an owner request and classify it as ledger, ARC, violation, or maintenance before a coordinator touches it; assemble a delinquency packet (ledger, notices, governing-document excerpt) for a human collections gate; build a board-meeting packet from recurring sources; chase vendor invoices that are stuck before AP close; and send a weekly digest of aged delinquencies and open building-register items.

Keep Condo Manager, or whatever CAM you choose, as the system of record for money and owner files. innflow is not a fake PMS and not a Condo Manager clone. Orchestrate the work around the ledger. Start with owner-request triage or board-packet assembly. Expand only after that path holds for a full billing cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Condo Manager good software for rental apartments?

Not as a primary rental PMS. Reviews and the feature set point to associations: owners, corporations, assessments, and building registers. Tenant portals, applications, and rental maintenance are the weak side. Use a rental system for doors you lease, and keep association accounting in a CAM tool.

How much does Condo Manager cost?

You have to request a quote. Published commentary has cited a start around $150 per month. Confirm implementation, processing, and community counts in writing. A free trial is available by contacting the vendor, not as an instant signup.

What should we short-list instead?

Self-managed boards: a published-price association tool such as PayHOA. Professional CAM firms: CINC, Vantaca, or Enumerate. Rental-heavy shops: a rental PMS, not an HOA ledger. Then add orchestration if the work still lives in email.

Can innflow replace Condo Manager?

No. innflow orchestrates workflows across systems of record. It does not replace assessment accounting, bank rec, or the official owner ledger. Keep the CAM. Automate the spine around it.

Is this a paid product review?

This is operator guidance for association and property teams. Pricing and features change. Verify every number on a current quote and a sandbox community before you buy.

Conclusion

Condo Manager HOA management software reviews come down to fit. The product is a user-friendly association back office with accrual accounting, owner files, meetings, and a building register. It is quote-priced, support and stability draw complaints, and it is a poor tenant system. Buy it for HOA work you can demonstrate in a demo. Do not buy it as a universal property platform.

When the ledger is chosen and the remaining pain is packets, routing, and exceptions, use innflow to connect tools and keep those flows visible. Get Started at innflow.ai or app.innflow.ai. Talk to Sales when you want the same operating cadence across every community you manage.

Condo Control is a building operating layer, not a rental ledger

High-rise condos and staffed associations do not fail first on the general ledger. They fail at the desk: visitor lists, packages, amenity bookings, incident logs, and the announcement that never reached the tower. Condo Control (often still called Condo Control Central) is built for that front-of-house and community-communication job. It is a weak answer if what you actually need is multifamily accounting, owner draws, and unit-turn work orders.

This condo control reviews pricing features and alternatives guide is for condo administrators, concierge and security leads, and management companies that run amenity-heavy buildings. You will see what the product covers, how Core versus Premium is sold, what users praise and criticize, and which alternatives belong on a short list. innflow is not a Condo Control clone. It orchestrates the work that still leaks around the resident app and the desk.

Buy the tool that matches the unit of work. If the unit of work is a package, a visitor, or a party-room booking, Condo Control is in the right category. If the unit of work is a rent ledger, keep reading until the alternatives section and do not force a concierge platform to become a PMS.

What Condo Control is in 2026

Condo Control is a web-based management and communication platform for condos, HOAs, boards, and the security or concierge firms that staff them. The product story is sync: residents, managers, and the desk share announcements, bookings, documents, and logs instead of clipboards and lobby whiteboards.

That story still holds. Amenity-heavy buildings added more of the same work: package volume, visitor QR codes, short-term-stay tracking, and after-hours incident reports. The 2026 question is not "does a resident portal exist." It is whether search, mobile, and multi-task stability hold when the desk is running packages, patrols, and bookings at the same time. Reviews are mixed on that last point.

Features that define the product

Communication

Announcements, a digital bulletin board, an events calendar, surveys, a file library, budget mail-outs, and e-delivery consent are the community layer. Residents get a portal and a mobile app. Managers get a resident database and unit files. This is the "keep the corporation informed" half of the product, and it is why self-managed boards look at Condo Control even when they do not have a full security desk.

Concierge, security, and the desk

This is the differentiator versus generic HOA software. The suite includes visitor tracking, guest tracking, parking and valet, key management, package management, security patrol, pass-on logs, security logs, and incident reports. Hardware is part of the offering, which is a real implementation project, not a software toggle. If you run a staffed lobby, evaluate this module in person with your actual desk workflow, not a marketing video.

Amenities, records, and service

Amenity and party-room booking, maintenance tracking, service requests and work orders, an online store, and online payments sit in the shared feature list. Architectural change requests, violation tracking, short and mid-term stay records, and lease details appear on Premium (or as Core add-ons). Record-keeping is framed as replacing paper forms. That only works if search works. Reviewers say it often does not.

Finance-adjacent tools

Condo Control can invoice, track balances, take payments and deposits, and handle purchase orders and vendor or procurement tasks on higher tiers. Treat this as operational finance around the building, not as a full association general ledger. If your CPA lives in a CAM accounting system, keep that system of record and ask how Condo Control posts or exports.

Condo Control pricing

Condo Control does not publish rates. Plans are commonly described as Core and Premium (some vendor materials also speak in Standard / Modern / Premium Living language). You request a quote. Multi-year discounts are advertised. First subscriptions typically include hardware and setup fees that are not shown until the proposal.

Both Core and Premium are described as including training (live webinars and videos), portfolio management, reporting, surveys, online status certificates, e-delivery consent, maintenance tracking, service requests, online store, online payments, budget mail-outs, file library, events, bulletin board, announcements, resident database, unit files, mobile app, and resident portal. A website may be included on Premium or sold as an add-on to Core.

Premium (or paid Core add-ons) is where desk and deeper operations live: incidents, valet, keys, parking, visitors, patrols, packages, bookings, ARC, violations, stays, lease details, invoicing, vendor management, assets, classifieds, forums, and voice or text alerts.

There is no free trial. There is a demo. That combination, plus unpublished price and setup fees, is the main procurement risk. You cannot cheaply test whether search and mobile friction will annoy your residents. Budget a paid pilot community and a written hardware list before you roll a portfolio.

What users praise and where they stall

Pros

  • Ease of use is the consistent compliment. Residents and staff can book amenities without a training class.
  • Customer success is well regarded. Teams report a named success manager and a path to request product changes.
  • The desk modules (packages, visitors, patrols) match how staffed condos actually work, which generic rental software does not.

Cons

  • Value is hard to judge because pricing is hidden and setup or hardware is extra. You buy after a demo, not after a trial.
  • Android users have reported extra clicks to reach announcements. That sounds small until it is every resident, every notice.
  • Search is a recurring complaint. Corporations with years of documents and events feel it first.
  • The product has been reported to crash or struggle when staff run many tasks at once: packages, security, amenities, and resident files in parallel. That is the exact moment you need the system.

None of those cons make Condo Control a bad desk product. They make implementation and device testing non-optional. If your building is mobile-first and document-heavy, put search and Android announcement paths in the demo script.

Alternatives, chosen by job, not by logo

PayHOA, HOA Start, and other published-price HOA tools

Self-managed associations that mainly need dues, documents, and a simple portal often do better with published pricing. PayHOA is commonly cited near $49 per month by unit tier. HOA Start is often cited near $39 per month. You give up concierge depth. You gain a price you can take to a volunteer board.

Buildium and rental-first PMS platforms

If the real book is rentals with a side of condo HOA work, a rental PMS with accounting, applications, and owner portals is the better system of record. Buildium's public plans have been listed from the high $50s to low $60s per month and up. Do not buy Condo Control as your accounting system and then bolt on rent collection later.

CINC, Vantaca, Enumerate

Management companies that need portfolio CAM accounting, lockbox, and board governance should short-list association platforms, then decide whether Condo Control still belongs at the desk of specific towers. Some buildings keep a concierge product next to a CAM ledger. That can be correct. Two full suites for one 40-unit walk-up is not.

Stessa and similar investor trackers are free or cheap for personal portfolios. They are not desk software. Landlord-mobile apps with a few units of paid storage are not Condo Control alternatives. Ignore them unless you are a single-building amateur landlord, in which case you do not need a security-desk platform.

How to run a Condo Control decision operationally

Name one owner: the regional manager or the building's operations lead. The board approves spend. Security contractors do not get to pick software that dumps a new login on the office.

Intake

Write the desk events you will measure: visitor check-in time, package scan to resident notice, amenity booking conflicts, incident-to-report cycle, announcement reach, and work-order intake. Require those fields in the demo. Bring live package volume and a month of incident types, not a happy-path tour.

Human gates

Hardware placement, data import of residents and vehicles, and the first week of live desk use need a human gate. So does any decision to put assessments or official ledgers only in Condo Control. Money and identity stay in systems your CPA and counsel can defend.

Exceptions

Design them: outage during a move-in Saturday, a crash while packages are stacked, a resident who never installed the app, a short-term renter who is not in the unit file, and a security vendor who will not use the patrol module. Each needs an owner, an SLA, and a paper or radio fallback.

Scoreboard

Desk cycle time, package aging, booking conflict rate, incident report completeness, support ticket age, and resident complaints about notices. Those decide if the product is earning the quote. A feature matrix from the RFP does not.

How innflow fits beside Condo Control

innflow is the AI agent and workflow automation platform built for real work. Agents connect to tools, run multi-step flows on a canvas, and keep execution visible. Condo Control can store the booking or the package. The work around it (after-hours escalation, board incident summaries, vendor follow-up, resident exceptions) still sits in email and radios.

Typical innflow patterns: classify an inbound resident message as booking, package, violation, or emergency and route it with an SLA; package an incident (photos, unit, time, desk notes) for a manager approval gate before it goes to the board or insurer; remind incomplete visitor or stay records; escalate packages that have sat past policy; and assemble a weekly operations digest the manager can actually read.

Keep Condo Control as the resident and desk system of record if you buy it. innflow is not a chatbot bolted onto the lobby and not a replacement PMS. Orchestrate the exceptions. Start with incident packets or package aging. Expand after one building holds for a full operating cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Condo Control publish pricing?

No. You request a quote for Core or Premium (and any hardware). There is no free trial. Budget setup fees and a pilot building before a portfolio rollout.

Who should actually buy Condo Control?

Staffed condos and HOAs that live on amenities, packages, visitors, and a security or concierge desk. Rental portfolio operators who need accounting and leasing should look at a PMS first and only add a desk product if a specific tower requires it.

What are the most common review complaints?

Hidden price, extra mobile clicks for announcements, weak search, and instability when staff run many modules at once. Ease of use and customer success are the usual compliments.

Can innflow replace Condo Control?

No. innflow orchestrates workflows across the systems you already run. It does not replace amenity calendars, package hardware, or the resident portal. Keep the building system. Automate the handoffs around it.

How should we compare alternatives?

Match the job. Published-price HOA tools for simple boards. CAM platforms for professional association accounting. A rental PMS for leased doors. Condo Control for the desk. Mixing those jobs in one RFP is how you buy the wrong stack.

Conclusion

Condo Control reviews, pricing, features, and alternatives come down to whether your bottleneck is the lobby and the resident app or the rental ledger. The product is strong on communication, bookings, packages, and security workflows, sold on unpublished Core and Premium quotes, and weaker on search, mobile friction, and high-concurrency stability. Buy it for staffed condo operations you can test in a real desk pilot.

When the building system is chosen and the remaining pain is routing, packets, and exceptions, use innflow to connect tools and keep those flows visible. Get Started at innflow.ai or app.innflow.ai. Talk to Sales when you want the same desk-to-office cadence across a portfolio of towers.

The move-in inspection is the deposit case you will try six months later

Most deposit disputes are not about the carpet. They are about a missing baseline. If you cannot prove what the unit looked like on day one, you are negotiating from memory against a tenant with phone photos. Completing move-in inspections is not a courtesy walkthrough. It is the legal and operational start of the tenancy: condition, keys, meters, safety devices, and the punch list that would otherwise become week-one emergency tickets.

This guide on completing move-in inspections tips landlords should actually use is for independent landlords, leasing agents, and maintenance leads who turn units under time pressure. You will get a room-by-room method, a photo standard, a sign-off process, and the handoff into work orders. It is not legal advice. Security-deposit statutes, notice rules, and required forms vary by state and city. Use a local lease and counsel for the form you put in front of the tenant.

The inspection is a workflow with an SLA: unit ready, tenant present or formally invited, report complete, photos stored, exceptions routed, keys released. innflow belongs on that spine. A clipboard in the leasing binder does not.

Why move-in inspections matter more in 2026

Turns are tighter. Applicants expect keys on the lease start date. Vendors miss windows. Teams skip the joint walk because "the make-ready looked fine." Then the tenant reports a stained ceiling, a dead outlet, and a missing screen on day two, and you have no dated file. Habitability complaints and deposit claims both start from that gap.

Several markets also tightened deposit handling: itemized deductions, statutory timelines, and photo evidence expectations. Even where the statute is quiet, a consistent inspection is how you treat tenants equally. Ad hoc walks ("we only inspect the units that look rough") is how you create a fair-housing story you did not intend.

Treat the inspection as part of make-ready close, not as a leasing afterthought. If the unit is not inspectable, it is not ready. Do not hand keys and promise to "catch the list later."

What a complete move-in inspection actually includes

A useful report is structured, dated, and signed. Free-text "unit in good condition" is worthless at move-out.

  • Identity of the file. Property, unit, lease start, inspector name, tenant names present, date and time.
  • Room-by-room condition. Ceiling, walls, trim, floors, windows, coverings, doors, hardware, lights, outlets, HVAC supply, and smoke or CO devices.
  • Systems and utilities. Meter readings if the tenant pays utilities, water heater, HVAC operation, appliances that stay, garage or storage, and exterior if the tenant maintains it.
  • Inventory. Keys, fobs, remotes, parking passes, manuals, filters, and any furniture that is included.
  • Safety. Detectors installed and tested, GFCI where you can reasonably check, lock function, railings, and any city-required items (window guards, extinguishers).
  • Exceptions. Every defect with a photo, an owner (make-ready vendor vs. tenant-caused vs. defer), and a due date.
  • Signatures. Tenant and landlord or agent. If the tenant refuses to sign, note that and still keep the file.

Use the same template on every unit in the portfolio. Customizing the form per building is fine. Inventing a new form per agent is how evidence falls apart.

A practical room-by-room sequence

Walk the unit the way a stranger would live in it, not the way the painter finished. Start outside if the tenant is responsible for any exterior, then work front door to back, then mechanicals.

Entry, halls, and living areas

Check door sweep, lock and deadbolt, peephole, and weatherstripping. Photograph each wall and the floor from two corners. Note nail holes, scuffs, and any patch that will telegraph later. Test every switch and outlet you can reach. Confirm window locks and screens. If there is a fireplace, photograph the condition and state whether it is in service or decorative only.

Kitchen

Run each burner or element briefly. Open the oven. Run the dishwasher a minute if it is provided. Check sink, sprayer, disposal, and shutoffs. Photograph counters, backsplash, cabinet interiors, and the floor at the sink. Look under the sink for moisture. Note the refrigerator model if it stays, and photograph existing shelves and door bins so "missing parts" is not a later argument.

Baths

Flush, fill, and drain. Check caulk lines, fan operation, GFCI, towel bars, and the underside of the sink. Photograph the tub or shower surround in a way that shows existing chips. Moisture and mold at move-in must be on the report even if you plan to treat them that week. Hidden moisture is a habitability issue, not a cosmetic note.

Bedrooms and closets

Same wall-and-floor photo standard. Test closets, rods, and doors that stick. Confirm egress windows operate. Photograph any remaining owner items so they do not become "tenant property" in a dispute.

Mechanicals, laundry, garage, and yard

Photograph the filter size and the current filter. Run heat or cool long enough to confirm air moves. Note the water-heater condition and any standing water. If laundry is included, run a short cycle or at least power on and photograph existing damage. For yards, photograph lawn, fence, and irrigation as you hand them over. Meter photos belong in this block when the tenant pays utilities.

Photo and video standards that hold up

Phones are enough if the process is consistent. Timestamped photos in a unit folder beat a cinematic walkthrough that never gets filed.

  • Wide shot of each wall, then close-ups of every defect.
  • Flooring in each room, especially seams and wet-area transitions.
  • Serial plates on appliances that stay.
  • Detector locations and a photo of a successful test if you can capture it.
  • Meter close-ups that are actually readable.
  • Keys and remotes on a counter before they leave with the tenant.

Do not store the only copy on the inspector's camera roll. Push to the property file the same day. If you record video, still pull stills of defects into the written report. Video that nobody names in the form will not be found when you need it.

How to run the inspection with the tenant

Invite the tenant to attend. A joint walk reduces "I never saw that stain" later. If they cannot attend, send the report and photos the same day and give a short written window to add comments. Some jurisdictions specify how move-in condition must be offered. Follow that rule even if your template is already good.

Walk slowly enough to let the tenant point things out. Add their items even when you disagree, then mark your disposition: will repair, pre-existing, tenant will monitor. Arguing them off the page is how you get a hostile occupancy on day one.

Do not release remaining keys until the report is signed or the refusal is documented, unless local practice or the lease says otherwise. If you must release keys because the lease started, complete the report before you leave the property. Completing it "from the office tomorrow" is how rooms get skipped.

Same-day, open work orders for anything that affects habitability or that you promised to fix. A punch list that lives only on the inspection PDF will die. The tenant should see a ticket number, not a smile and a verbal "we'll get that."

Deposits, keys, and the legal edges (not legal advice)

The inspection file is what lets you deduct for damage above ordinary wear at move-out. Ordinary wear is not a hole in the door. A two-year-old carpet with even traffic is usually wear. Photograph both so you are not guessing later. Follow your state's rules on deposit amounts, separate accounts, and itemization deadlines. The inspection does not create a right to deduct that the statute does not allow.

If the unit fails a safety check (no working smoke detector, no hot water, active leak), it is not a successful move-in. Either delay occupancy or document a written repair SLA the tenant accepts. Handing keys on a failed unit to "start rent" is how you buy a rent-escrow or inspector visit.

Fair housing applies to how you inspect. Same form, same photo standard, same repair priority rules. Do not inspect more harshly because you dislike the applicant you just approved.

How to run move-in inspections as an operation

Name one process owner, usually the leasing manager or the make-ready supervisor. Shared ownership is how Saturday move-ins happen with no inspector.

Intake

Every approved lease creates an inspection task with a time window, assigned inspector, unit status (ready or not), and required fields. If make-ready is not complete, the inspection does not get scheduled as "done on arrival." It gets scheduled as a fail path.

Human gates

A clean, complete report can flow automatically into the tenant file. A habitability fail, a tenant refusal to sign, a large pre-existing damage claim, or a request to move in early needs a human gate. Do not let an agent waive the inspection to save a concession.

Exceptions

Design them: tenant no-show, unit still has vendors on site, lockout after hours, pet already in the unit, utility not transferred so you cannot test HVAC, and a non-English-speaking tenant who needs the form explained. Each exception needs an owner, an SLA, and a packet (lease, photos, vendor status).

Scoreboard

Percent of move-ins with a signed report on day one, hours from keys to photos in the file, punch-list items closed inside the promised SLA, day-seven tickets that should have been on the inspection, and deposit claims lost for missing baseline evidence. Those measures change staffing. A count of "inspections completed" does not.

How innflow fits move-in inspections

innflow is the AI agent and workflow automation platform built for real work. Agents connect to tools, run multi-step flows on a canvas, and keep execution visible. Move-in inspection is a multi-step path: lease signed, unit ready, inspector assigned, report captured, photos stored, exceptions ticketed, keys confirmed. That is orchestration, not a chatbot in the hallway.

Typical innflow patterns: create the inspection task when the lease is fully executed; block key release if required fields are empty; attach photo folders to the unit file; open work orders from checked defects with the photo already attached; remind the tenant of the comment window if they did not attend; and send a daily digest of tomorrow's move-ins that are not actually ready.

Keep your PMS or maintenance system as the record for the unit and the tickets. innflow orchestrates the handoff so the inspection is not a PDF lost in someone's downloads. Start with same-day filing and habitability fails. Expand after one full turn cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should the tenant be present for the move-in inspection?

Yes, whenever you can make it happen. A joint walk produces a better list and a harder file to dispute. If they cannot attend, send the dated report and photos immediately and invite written additions inside a short window that matches your lease and local rules.

How long should a move-in inspection take?

Long enough to photograph every room and test the systems you are handing over. A studio might be fifteen to twenty minutes. A house with yard, garage, and appliances can run forty-five minutes or more. If you are done in five minutes, you did a greeting, not an inspection.

Can I use a video instead of a written checklist?

Video is useful evidence. It is not a substitute for a structured report the tenant can sign. Pull defects into the written form so they are named, not buried in a twenty-minute file nobody will rewatch.

What if the unit is not ready on move-in day?

Do not pretend. Document the fails, delay keys if you legally can, or obtain a written repair SLA for each habitability item. Opening a tenancy on an unfinished unit without a file is how you lose both the relationship and the deposit case.

Is this legal advice?

No. Deposit statutes, required inspection forms, and entry rules differ by jurisdiction. Have counsel review the form and the key-release rule you use in each state you operate.

Conclusion

Completing move-in inspections, tips landlords should not skip, is simple on paper: same template, dated photos, tenant voice on the page, same-day tickets, keys only when the file exists. The teams that still lose deposit cases are the ones that treated the walk as optional hospitality. The teams that stay calm at move-out already have the day-one file.

When you are ready to run inspections as a visible workflow instead of a clipboard, use innflow to connect tools, enforce the required fields, and keep punch-list handoffs on the canvas. Get Started at innflow.ai or app.innflow.ai. Talk to Sales when you want the same inspection standard across every community you turn.

OER is a efficiency test, not a trophy number

An operating expense ratio calculator will happily give you a percentage. It will not tell you whether you booked a capital roof as an expense, whether you used asking rent instead of collected rent, or whether last year's insurance spike made a good building look broken. Operators who treat OER as a single pass/fail score buy the wrong asset or fire the wrong manager.

This complete guide using operating expense ratio tools is for landlords, portfolio managers, and asset leads who need the formula, the inputs, a clean example, and a way to use the result next to cap rate and cash flow. It is not accounting or investment advice. Chart-of-accounts policy and lender definitions control. Align with your CPA before you put OER in an offering memo.

Once you know the math, the work is monthly: pull expenses, exclude the right items, lock income, and flag properties that moved. innflow belongs on that close and exception path. A one-off spreadsheet does not keep a portfolio honest.

What operating expense ratio is, and why it still matters in 2026

Operating expense ratio (OER) compares what it costs to run a property with the income that property produces. It is usually expressed as a percentage: the share of gross operating income consumed by operating expenses. A lower OER means more of each rent dollar survives operations. A higher OER means the building is expensive to run, the income is weak, or the books are messy.

In 2026 the inputs are noisier. Insurance, taxes, and contract labor moved faster than rent in many markets. That can lift OER even when the on-site team is competent. The ratio is still useful if you compare like to like: same product type, same trailing twelve months, same treatment of vacancy and capital items. It is not useful as a national league table.

Use OER with other measures. Cap rate speaks to price versus net operating income. Cash flow after debt service speaks to whether the note works. Occupancy and concession rates explain the income side. OER explains operating load. None of them replace a rent roll and a general ledger.

The formula a calculator is actually running

The common real-estate form is:

OER = (Total operating expenses minus annual depreciation) divided by gross operating income

Some textbooks write OER as operating expenses divided by effective gross income and handle depreciation separately. Calculators aimed at rental investors often subtract depreciation because it is a non-cash accounting charge, not a vendor bill. Whatever you choose, write the definition at the top of the model and do not switch it mid-portfolio.

Operating expenses

Include the costs required to keep the property operating in the period: property taxes, insurance, property management fees, repairs and maintenance, landscaping, pest control, owner-paid utilities, turnover costs that you treat as operating, resident screening if you expense it, and similar recurring items. Do not drop in mortgage principal. Debt service is not an operating expense. Do not drop in capital improvements you have elected to capitalize (a new roof, a full HVAC replacement) if your policy says those sit on the balance sheet.

Mixed books are the usual error. One asset manager expenses unit turns. Another capitalizes them. Their OERs are not comparable until someone normalizes the policy.

Depreciation

Depreciation is the periodic write-down of the building and other depreciable assets. It is real for tax and book income. It is not cash leaving the operating account this month. Many OER calculators subtract annual depreciation from operating expenses so the ratio reflects cash operating load. If your source expenses already exclude depreciation, do not subtract it again.

Gross operating income

Gross operating income (GOI) is the income the property earned, or is expected to earn, before operating expenses. For residential rentals that is usually scheduled rent plus other income (parking, laundry, pet rent) minus vacancy and credit loss if you are using effective gross income. Commercial assets may have recoveries and other income that belong in the same stack. Be explicit: are you using trailing collected income, trailing billed income, or pro forma market rent? Acquisition models that use optimistic asking rent will print a prettier OER than the building can deliver.

A worked example you can re-run by hand

Use a complete trailing twelve months, not a toy expense line. Two similar apartments in the same year:

Apartment A. Collected rent and other income (GOI) is $2,500 times 12, or $30,000. Operating expenses (taxes, insurance, management, maintenance, owner-paid utilities) total $18,000. Depreciation on the building portion is $6,000 and is not inside the $18,000 cash operating total. OER on a cash-operating definition is $18,000 / $30,000 = 60 percent. If your calculator subtracts depreciation from a book-expense total that already includes it, do that subtraction once. Do not subtract $6,000 from $18,000 unless depreciation was booked inside that $18,000.

Apartment B. GOI is $2,300 times 12, or $27,600. The same fixed stack plus a unit repaint that your policy treats as operating brings expenses to $21,000. OER is $21,000 / $27,600 = about 76 percent. B looks worse because it has less income and more operating work in the same year. If the repaint is truly a capital improvement under your policy, take it out of OER and the ratio falls. If you always run turns through operations, leave it in and label the year a turn year so next year's comparison is fair.

These figures are an illustration of the arithmetic, not a benchmark for your market. Taxes and insurance alone can consume a large share of GOI. Rebuild from your ledger.

Run your own numbers with a complete T12:

  • Sum operating expenses from the ledger (policy-clean).
  • Subtract depreciation only if it is inside that sum and your definition requires it.
  • Divide by GOI or EGI, stated on the same period.
  • Express as a percentage.

What is a "good" OER?

Lower is better, all else equal. There is no single healthy number. Published ranges often put residential properties somewhere around 60 to 80 percent when the stack is fully loaded, industrial assets much lower (sometimes cited under 20 percent), and office or retail somewhere in a 20 to 60 percent band. Those bands are directional. A Class A high-rise with union staff and a loaded amenity deck will not print like a triple-net industrial box. A single-family rental with owner-paid landscaping and aging HVAC will not print like a new garden community with RUBS.

Compare:

  • The same property to itself, trailing twelve versus prior trailing twelve.
  • Sister assets of the same vintage and service level.
  • A purchase T12 against your own chart of accounts, not the broker's recast until you have tested it.

A sudden jump often means insurance, taxes, utilities, or a maintenance event. A sudden drop can mean deferred maintenance, a missing accrual, or income you will not collect. Investigate both. Do not celebrate a low OER you cannot explain.

When to use the calculator (and when to ignore it)

Acquisitions. Recast the seller T12 with your insurance quote, your tax assumption, your payroll, and your turnover standards. Then calculate OER. If the deal only works on the seller's understated expenses, you do not have a deal.

Portfolio monitoring. Rank assets by OER and by change in OER. The list is a conversation starter for the regional manager, not an automatic capital event.

Budgeting. A budget that implies an OER the property has never hit needs a story: RUBS rollout, staff reduction, or insurance shopping. If there is no story, the budget is fiction.

Do not use OER alone to: set rent (use comps and renewal math), choose a loan (use DSCR and lender definitions), or fire a manager (use a scoreboard that includes delinquencies, occupancy, and work-order cycle time). OER can be the clue. It is rarely the verdict.

How to run OER as an accounting operation

Name one process owner, usually the controller or the asset-management analyst. Shared ownership is how two regions report two different OERs for the same chart of accounts.

Intake

Every property-month needs structured fields: GOI definition, expense total, depreciation treatment, known one-time items, and whether the period is closed. Spreadsheet tabs named "final_v7" are not intake.

Human gates

A routine monthly calc can be automated. Recasts for acquisitions, any restatement of a prior period, and any public or lender-facing OER need a human gate. So does reclassifying a large invoice from expense to capex after the ratio already went to leadership.

Exceptions

Design them: missing utility bills, a tax reassessment, an insurance bind mid-year, a casualty year, a property that switched management companies and charts, and a T12 that includes related-party fees you will not pay. Each exception needs an owner, an SLA, and a packet (ledger export, invoice, policy note).

Scoreboard

Days to close, properties with OER change beyond your threshold, properties with incomplete T12s, and the count of manual journal adjustments after first close. Those measures improve the calculator's inputs. A dashboard of green percentages does not.

How innflow fits OER and monthly close

innflow is the AI agent and workflow automation platform built for real work. Agents connect to tools, run multi-step flows on a canvas, and keep execution visible. OER fails when intake is late or inconsistent. That is a workflow problem sitting on top of the general ledger, not a reason to buy another calculator widget.

Typical innflow patterns: pull a closed-period expense and income pack from the accounting system; flag accounts that look like capex sitting in repairs; request the missing utility invoice before close; assemble an acquisition recast checklist (insurance quote, tax card, payroll, turnover assumptions); and send asset managers a weekly digest of properties whose OER moved more than the threshold, with the contributing accounts attached.

Keep the PMS or accounting system as the system of record. innflow orchestrates the close and the exception path. It is not a general ledger and not a replacement for your CPA. Start with "T12 complete and defined" for one product type. Expand after a full close cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is mortgage payment part of operating expenses?

No. Principal and interest are financing costs. They matter for cash flow and DSCR. They do not belong in OER. Property taxes and insurance do belong if the owner pays them as operating items.

Should I subtract depreciation?

Only if depreciation is inside the expense total and your written definition says OER is a cash operating load. If the ledger already excludes depreciation, subtracting again understates the ratio. Pick one definition and keep it.

Why does my OER look nothing like the 60 to 80 percent residential band?

Your expense stack may be incomplete, your income may be gross scheduled rent with no vacancy, or your product type may not match the band. Rebuild from the T12 before you decide the property is a star or a problem.

Can an AI agent calculate OER for the whole portfolio?

It can assemble the pack and apply a stated formula after close. It should not invent a recast or hide a reclass. innflow is built for that split: agents on intake and packaging, humans on definition changes and lender-facing numbers.

Is this accounting advice?

No. GAAP, tax, and lender reporting can require different treatments of the same invoice. Agree the definition with your CPA and, if relevant, your lender, then automate that definition.

Conclusion

A complete guide using operating expense ratio starts with a written formula, clean inputs, and the humility to pair the percentage with cash flow and the rent roll. Calculators are fast. Bad GOI and mixed capex policy are faster. Operators who win on OER are the ones who close the month the same way every time and investigate the properties that moved.

When you are ready to run that close and exception path as a visible workflow, use innflow to connect tools, assemble the packs, and keep handoffs on the canvas. Get Started at innflow.ai or app.innflow.ai. Talk to Sales when you want the same OER operating cadence across the portfolio.
